activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: The Gulf Stream leaves the US coast near Cape Hatteras, North Carolina, and turns northeast across the Atlantic.
story:
The map kept slipping in the wind, and Ashley kept pinning it flat with her water bottle while Leighton held the corners like it was a crime scene photograph. They had chosen the far end of the boardwalk, where the tide came in over the sand in long, unhurried sweeps, because Mr. Ong had said their oceanography presentation had to happen outside, at the shore, by four o'clock, or he would not sign off on the unit. It was a strange rule, but then Mr. Ong was a strange teacher, the kind who cajoled his students into things by insisting they were already doing them.

"Okay," Leighton said. "Go from the top. Because last time you said the warm current goes north and then you just pointed at Canada."

"That was a rough draft." Ashley smoothed the paper. The colored arrows arced across the printed Atlantic, red and blue, and she had spent two evenings on the kitchen floor tracing the red one with her finger until her mother asked if she was praying. "The warm one is the Gulf Stream. Watch where it leaves us." She set her finger on the coastline. "See Cape Hatteras? North Carolina. That's where it turns away from the coast and heads northeast across the Atlantic. Toward Europe."

Hunter, sprawled on the sand with his shoes off, raised a hand like he was in class. "Question. Why does it leave at North Carolina and not, like, New Jersey? New Jersey is right there asking for warmth."

The honest answer was that Ashley did not entirely know, and she said so, which surprised her. Last spring she would have invented something confident and thin, a veneer of expertise over a hole, because in eighth grade she had given a talk on photosynthesis using the word "sun food" and a boy named Marcus had never let it go. She remembered standing at the front of that classroom, ears burning, deciding that never again would she admit a gap out loud.

"Nobody told me why," she said now, "so I'm not going to make something up. What I can tell you is where. It leaves the coast near Cape Hatteras, in North Carolina, and it turns northeast across the Atlantic. That part I could draw in my sleep. It's why Britain is warmer than places in Canada at the same latitude. The warm water carries heat over."

"Carries heat," Hunter repeated, in the tone of a man discovering a scandal. "So the ocean is doing my job for me. I was going to mail a sweater to Scotland."

Leighton laughed, and Ashley checked her phone. Three twelve. They had forty-eight minutes, and Mr. Ong had promised to walk down from the parking lot at four sharp, impecunious thermos in hand, as he put it, claiming he'd spent his last dollars on the laminating of these very maps. That was the joke he made every semester, and every semester somebody looked up the word afterward and felt quietly betrayed.

They ran it twice more. The tide crept closer and they retreated up the sand, dragging backpacks, Hunter refusing to put his shoes on out of principle. Leighton played the part of a confused European, asking why her winters were so mild, and Ashley answered with the red arrow and the turn at Hatteras, and the second time through she stopped hedging. She still could not say why the current left the coast exactly there. She could say what it did, and that it did it every year without asking anyone's permission, and she found she preferred the solid outline of a true thing to the soft blur of a guessed one. Maybe, she thought, knowing the edge of your knowledge was not the same as being ignorant. Maybe it was the opposite.

At three fifty-eight a figure appeared at the top of the boardwalk, moving with the unhurried certainty of a man who believed he was early even when he was late. Mr. Ong came down the ramp with sand already on his shoes, as if he had been at the beach all his life, and stopped in front of their map, which the wind had just now chosen to flip entirely over.

"Start," he said. "And Ashley, this time, begin where the current leaves the coast."

She turned the map right side up, set her finger on North Carolina, and began.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: For an accurate reading, a person should sit quietly for about five minutes with feet flat and the arm supported at heart level, because posture and activity change the numbers.
story:
The manual sat open on the kitchen table between a bowl of cold oatmeal and his mother's unread mail, and Aaron had read the same paragraph four times without retaining a word of it. He was eighteen, finished with high school in June, and enrolled to start a patient care assistant course in the fall, which meant that by August he had to pass a basic health screening of his own knowledge, including reading a blood pressure number off a cuff and saying, out loud, what it meant and how a person's habits could move it. His grandfather had frightened the whole family in April when a pharmacy machine had told him something alarming, and nobody had known whether to believe it, and Aaron had decided, quietly and without announcing it, that he would be the one in the family who knew.

Mr. Johansson from two doors down had a cuff of his own, an old manual one, and had brought it over in a grocery bag along with a sack of plums from the tree in his backyard. "That arboreal monster produces more than I can eat," he said, setting the plums by the sink. "Take some to your mother." He was seventy-six and walked every morning and took no medication, which Aaron found quietly impressive and a little mysterious, like a man who had won an argument with his own body decades ago and never mentioned it again.

The trouble began with Aaron himself. He had run up the stairs with the cuff under his arm, out of breath and annoyed about something trivial, and he strapped it on right away to practice, and the number that came up did not augur anything good. He took it again immediately, standing, and it was higher still, and for a full minute he sat at the kitchen table imagining the screening in August, imagining the instructor's face, imagining a future rerouted.

Alessandro showed up around then, letting himself in the back door the way he had since they were ten. He looked at the numbers Aaron had written in the margin of the manual and whistled, not helpfully. "That's not your number," Alessandro said. "I did the machine at the pharmacy last month, the one by the register. I'd basically jogged in from the parking lot. It gave me something crazy. Then I sat in their little waiting chair and did the crossword on my phone for a while and tried again, and it was way lower."

"Sitting changed it?"

"Sitting still changed it. I was doing nothing, feet on the floor, for a few minutes. The pharmacist said that's how it's supposed to be done." Alessandro shrugged as though this were obvious, but Aaron was already flipping back through the manual, and there it was in the fine print he had skimmed: sit quietly for about five minutes, feet flat, arm supported at heart level, because posture and activity change the numbers.

"Posture and activity," Aaron said. "So my number is real, but it's the number for a guy who just ran upstairs and is standing in his own kitchen being scared about it."

"It's the number for a guy who needs to sit down," Alessandro said, and took a plum.

So Aaron sat. He put both feet flat on the kitchen floor, rested his arm on the table with the cuff level with his heart, and set a timer for five minutes, and the two of them sat there without talking, which was a kind of friendship they had practiced for years, and outside a sprinkler ticked across Mr. Johansson's lawn. When the timer went off Aaron inflated the cuff again, watched the needle settle, and wrote the new number down beside the old ones. It was lower. It was, he suspected, actually his.

Azaan came by that evening for the reason he always came by, which was that his aunt made too much food and regarded Aaron's household as a charity case, and he ended up staying when he heard what they were doing. He was the one who pushed the second half of the problem. "Fine, you can get the number," Azaan said, leaning against the counter with a container of rice in his hands. "But the screening wants you to say what it means. What actually moves it? You can't just read off a number like a scoreboard."

Aaron had the packet from the course, and they spread it out and argued their way through it. Salt was the thing everyone knew about, and the packet said less of it, more vegetables and fruits, less processed food, and regular exercise, the aerobic kind, most days. "Like Mr. Johansson," Aaron said. "He walks every morning and eats off his own tree, and his number is better than mine probably is." Azaan pointed out that this proved nothing about one man, and Aaron conceded the point, because it was true; one neighbor was a story, not evidence, and he did not yet know enough to say which habits mattered most or how much. What he could say honestly was that the reading was a snapshot, the habits were the weather, and a person could change the weather.

The indemnity of his ignorance, he thought later, was that he had been paying it out for years in family panic, in the April afternoon when his grandfather's pharmacy reading had sent three phone calls racing through the family like current through wire. His grandfather had sat in that pharmacy chair for maybe forty seconds, if that, before the machine squeezed his arm, having walked in from a hot parking lot carrying bags.

On Sunday his grandfather came for dinner, and after the dishes Aaron set him up at the kitchen table, feet flat on the floor, arm resting on a folded towel at the level of his heart, and they sat together for five quiet minutes while the kitchen clock went and his grandfather complained, gently, that this was a lot of ceremony for a rubber tube. "The numbers change depending on how you're sitting and what you were just doing," Aaron said. "That's why we wait." He took the reading, wrote it down, and slid the paper across the table, and then he said what he had decided to say plainly, that the number was better than April's, that walking and the food they were already eating were part of why, and that he would take it again in a month, same chair, same five minutes.

His grandfather looked at the number for a long moment, then at Aaron, then folded the paper once and put it in his shirt pocket.

"Again in a month," he said. "Same chair."

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: A video cannot be reverse-searched directly by most image engines, so fact-checkers take screenshots of key frames and search those images instead.
story:
My grandmother's house smells like pencil shavings and basil, which is a combination I have always considered sophisticated, the way I consider most things about this house sophisticated, including the antiquated rotary phone in the hallway that no one has dialed since roughly the Bronze Age. I am spending the last week of summer here because our apartment is being repainted, which is the official story, and because my mother and I are not speaking about the thing we are not speaking about, which is a different story. This morning I am on the back porch with Kurtis, who came over supposedly to help my grandfather restack firewood and has so far absconded from all stacking duties, and Sonia, who is here because she is always here.

The video arrives the way these things arrive, without ceremony. Kurtis plays it on his phone and holds it out like evidence at a trial. It shows a flooded street, a man wading past a floating car, and a caption claiming it is our city, downtown, this week. "Bro," Kurtis says, in the tone of a person who has just discovered something enormous, "my cousin posted it, it's like two blocks from the YMCA."

I watch it three times. The water looks real. The car looks real. My first instinct, and I want to be honest about my instincts here, is to share it immediately, because I pride myself on being the person in our group who passes along important information first. Sonia, who has been peeling an orange with surgical patience, says, "It's not raining here." This is her contribution. She considers it decisive. I consider it insufficient, because everyone knows weather varies, and I say so, magnanimously.

But something nags at me. I took a media literacy module last spring that I mostly slept through, except for one phrase that stuck: reverse image search. The idea is that you can trace a picture back to its origins, find out where it first appeared, when, whether it has been recycled. I decide to do this, partly out of genuine civic responsibility and partly because I want to be the one who finds out first, and I announce this to the porch. "I'm going to reverse-search it," I say, with the gravity of a detective donning a coat.

Here is where I run into my first wall, which I handle gracefully by staring at my phone for ten minutes. The video will not search. I drag it into the image search box and the engine refuses it, politely, the way a bouncer refuses a fake ID. I try a different engine. Same refusal. Kurtis watches over my shoulder and offers commentary. "Maybe the internet is broken," he says, which is his genus of observation, the kind that sounds like a joke and is actually a sincere theory.

Then Sonia leans over, still holding half an orange, and says the thing that changes the afternoon. "Screenshot it. A key frame. Then search the picture." I look at her. She shrugs. "My cousin does fact-checking stuff. A video can't go in directly, so they grab a screenshot of a key frame and search that instead." It is the most technical sentence Sonia has ever produced, and she delivers it like she is telling us where the bus stop is.

I pause on the frame where the floating car is clearest, screenshot it, and drop the image into the search bar. It works instantly, which is almost insulting. The results stack up: the same street, the same car, the same man, from a flood in a different state, three years ago. Three years. The caption on the viral version said this week. I sit back and feel the particular satisfaction of a person who has caught a lie, and also a smaller, quieter feeling underneath it, which is that I nearly shared the thing myself, five minutes ago, with full confidence, and that my confidence has historically not been a reliable instrument. I hold both of those at once, the triumph and the doubt, and I do not resolve them, because they are both true.

Mr. Russo, the neighbour whose fence shares our porch view, has been watering his tomatoes through all of this, apparently deaf to the entire drama. He calls across the yard, "Is that the flood from the news?" and I stand up to tell him no, it's old, it's from three years ago, and as I'm explaining the screenshot trick with more authority than I've earned, Kurtis quietly hits share on something else, a clip of a shark swimming down a highway. "This one's definitely real though," he says.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Sociologist Ray Oldenburg's 1989 book The Great Good Place named 'third places', such as cafes and libraries, where people meet outside home and work.
story:
The boxes in Alice's room had been unpacked for three weeks, which was long enough that she could no longer claim the move was temporary. Her father called it "settling in," the way adults eulogize a loss by giving it a nicer name. In the old town she had walked to Morgane's house in eleven minutes, and Vicky had kept a spare house key in her coat pocket all winter in case Alice's parents worked late. Here, the nearest classmate lived forty minutes away by a bus that ran twice an hour and stopped at five.

She tried the coffee place on Miller Street first, because it had a chalkboard and squashy chairs, the kind of place where people presumably became friends. She bought a hot chocolate, sat for an hour, and watched two women share a table without speaking, each guarding her laptop like a diplomat's briefcase. Nobody looked at her. The chair emitted a smell of wet wool every time she shifted. She left the hot chocolate half finished and decided the problem was the chairs.

The public library was closer, and warmer, and had a long oak table by the window with a lamp that worked. On her second afternoon there she claimed the corner seat and read for her English class, and on the third afternoon the same elderly man was in the opposite corner doing a crossword, and on the fourth a boy from her civics class, whose name she thought was Dev, nodded at her from the far end. The radiator under the table ticked like a slow clock. The window smelled faintly of rain on pavement. By the end of the week, the librarian with the headscarf, Ms. Karimi, had stopped asking for her card.

"Give it two months," her father said at dinner. "You'll have people." He said it the way he said the refrigerator would pay for itself, with confidence borrowed from somewhere else.

In civics, the teacher put a quote on the board about community and asked what made a place where strangers become neighbors. Dev raised his hand and said, "My mom's always going on about this. Sociologist Ray Oldenburg, 1989, The Great Good Place. He called them third places. Not home, not work or school. Cafes, libraries, barbershops. Where people actually meet." The teacher wrote "third places" on the board, and Alice copied it into her margin and then wrote underneath, not for the class, Miller Street, failed, and then, library, working?

Because something was happening at the library, though she was cautious about calling it what her father would call it. The crossword man, whose name turned out to be Rolf, had begun to slide a section of the paper toward her when he was done with it, and he complained about the paper's obsolescent TV listings in a stage whisper that made Ms. Karimi look over her glasses. Dev sat at the table most Tuesdays and Thursdays. He was trying to get the chess club reinstated and needed a faculty sponsor, which was, he admitted, "a recidivism problem, the way principals keep cancelling it and it keeps coming back and getting cancelled again." Alice laughed before she could stop herself, and he looked pleased.

She tested the idea against Morgane over video call, because Morgane was the person who argued with her until one of them changed her mind. "It's not the same," Morgane said, eating cereal on camera. "I could tell you a third place is anywhere, my bus stop is a third place, and you'd be wrong on the technicality. Home's first, work's second, and it's Oldenburg's actual term, so it has a definition. It's not just vibes." Alice said she knew that, she'd looked it up, she wasn't making it into a metaphor. "Good," Morgane said, "because you do that. You eulogize things until they mean whatever you need them to mean." That stung precisely because Vicky had once said something similar, in kinder words, at a sleepover in October.

Alice thought about it on the walk home, past the coffee place, whose windows glowed the same warm yellow as the library's. What she had not worked out was whether the table was a place she belonged to or only a place she occupied, and whether those were different, and whether friendship that began with a shared radiator could survive the fact that she might move again in two years if her father's contract renewed. Rolf would still be there. Dev would presumably still be chasing a chess sponsor through the administration like a man chasing his own hat. She could be a regular or she could be a passerby, and both were honest options, and she did not yet know which she was choosing.

On Thursday she brought the civics reading to the table and set it down in the corner seat. Rolf folded his crossword to the crease and peered at her book. "That looks grim," he said. Dev pulled out a battered chess set, missing a bishop's head, and set up the pieces on the far end without asking. Ms. Karimi wheeled the returned-books cart past and slowed down just enough to say, "Corner seat's yours, Alice. I've labeled it in my head." Alice sat, moved a pawn forward two squares, and said, "That's a third place thing to say."

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: A plagal cadence moves from the IV chord to the I chord and is often called the 'Amen cadence' because many hymns sing 'Amen' to it.
story:
Madeline had the assignment under control. That was the story she told Martha on Tuesday, and again on Wednesday, and by Thursday she had almost habituated herself to believing it: sixteen bars, chord changes, standard notation, due at the start of Friday's class, and hers was, as she said, basically done. What was actually done was a title, "Harbor," and four bars of melody that wandered between two notes like a gull refusing to commit to a piling. The rest of the manuscript paper on the music room stand was blank in a way that seemed to grow louder the longer she looked at it.

The music room stayed open until five on Thursdays because Mr. Côté ran jazz band, and after the trumpets left he let two or three students keep working at the upright pianos in the corner. Madeline had claimed one, Charlie-Rose the other. Charlie-Rose was writing something in F major with actual chords pencilled under the staff, changes every two bars, sensible and unhurried, and Madeline found her presence both steadying and faintly unbearable.

"Yours sounds like a question that forgot the question," Charlie-Rose said, not unkindly, when Madeline played her four bars for the fourth time.

"It's minimalist," Madeline said. "Repetition is a technique." This was true of the four bars, anyway, if not of her assertion that the piece was finished. She had a talent for selecting facts that flattered her and discarding the rest, and she knew it, which was the inconvenient part.

The problem was the ending. She could get to bar twelve now, a melody that arched up and settled, but every time she tried to close it, the final chord felt like a door swung shut in an empty hallway. Her last change, from the dominant back home, was correct, textbook, and it sounded like a textbook. She pressed the same progression again, softer, and it soured further the more she apologized for it with her touch.

That evening her grandfather was in the kitchen humming while he dried dishes, the way he did, some hymn from the church of his childhood that he only half remembered. At the end he landed on two chords and sang a small, satisfied "Amen," and Madeline, standing in the doorway with her notebook, felt something shift in her ear. The movement under that word was different from hers. It wasn't the dominant pulling the tonic into line; it was the subdominant, a gentler chord, laying the home chord down beside it like a blanket rather than snapping it shut. She sat at the kitchen table, wrote IV, then I, and played it on the out-of-tune piano in the hallway while her grandfather hummed the last phrase over her shoulder, twice, approving.

Friday morning, before class, she showed Charlie-Rose the ending in the music room. Charlie-Rose played it, frowned, played it again, and then grinned. "That's the Amen cadence," she said. "IV going to I. Half the hymns ever written sing 'Amen' right there." Madeline had known it sounded right; she had not known it had a name, and the name made it hers in a different way, a thing she had found in a kitchen and could now carry into a classroom. She copied the chords into her manuscript in her neatest ink, all sixteen bars, and only then noticed the clock. Mr. Côté was already stacking his notes at the front.

Her grade, when it came back the following week, was a B, with a note in red at the bottom: "Bars 9 to 12 sit on one chord too long; the harmony stops moving. The ending, however, is lovely." Madeline read that sentence four times, deciding each time how to feel about it, and arrived nowhere definite. She had wanted the piece to prove she was in control, and it had instead proved something more mixed: that she had been bluffing, that the bluff had driven her to a kitchen piano, and that the discovery at the end belonged to her more honestly than the four confident bars at the beginning ever had. Whether she would start the next assignment earlier was a question she left carefully open, even to herself.

She found Charlie-Rose at lunch and laid the marked page on the table between their trays. "Bars nine to twelve," Madeline said, and played the lazy stretch of the line against the table edge with two fingers. "I think I know what it wants instead."

"Show me," Charlie-Rose said, already closing her sandwich bag.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Aristotle named three means of persuasion: ethos, the speaker's credibility; pathos, the audience's emotions; and logos, the logic of the argument.
story:
The back booth of the Golden Lotus had the best acoustics, Matthew had decided, and the worst lighting, and he needed both, so on the slow Tuesday between lunch and dinner he commandeered it with his backpack, his phone, and a pot of tea he had no intention of drinking. Eliott slid in across from him with a stack of index cards, and Sally arrived ten minutes later, still in her soccer jacket, dropping into the booth with the air of someone who expected to be bored but was willing to be persuaded otherwise.

"Five minutes," Matthew said. "Entirely in Spanish. Friday. On whether the city should ban cars from the downtown core." He laid the phone flat between the napkin dispenser and the soy sauce. "Mr. Ferreira timed a boy last year who switched to English for one verb and marked him down a whole grade."

"So practice," Sally said. "Go. I'll count."

He went. He had prepared seven arguments, and he delivered them in order, each one a small brick laid on the last: emissions figures, the Copenhagen study, the accident statistics on Fourth Street, the projected drop in asthma admissions. His accent held. His verb tenses, mostly, held. When the timer chimed he sat back, and the somnolence of the big lunch his mother had made him eat settled over the booth like a lid.

Eliott was frowning at the index cards, flipping through them one at a time. "You said the same thing seven ways," he said.

"That's the point. Evidence."

"No, I mean." Eliott turned his phone around and read off the screen. "Aristotle named three means of persuasion: ethos, the speaker's credibility; pathos, the audience's emotions; and logos, the logic of the argument." He set the phone down. "Every card you have is the third one. All of them. You've got no ethos, no pathos, just a stack of facts."

"That's what an argument is," Matthew said, but even as he said it the sentence felt thinner than he wanted it to. Sally had leaned forward, chin on her fist, watching him with an expression he recognized from history seminars, the one that meant she was about to take the other side for sport.

"Tell me again why cars should be banned," she said, "but this time tell me like you're talking to my grandmother, who takes the bus to her dialysis appointments and still can't get across the street to the clinic because of the traffic."

He opened his mouth to recite the Copenhagen study. What came out instead, after a stalled second, was slower: "Mi abuela cruzó esa calle cada día durante veinte años," he tried, "y ahora tiene miedo." My grandmother crossed that street every day for twenty years, and now she is afraid. His own grandmother had never crossed Fourth Street in her life, and the sentence startled him anyway, the way it did something the statistics had not.

"There," Sally said. "That's half of it. Now the other half. Why should your audience believe you and not the man with the parking lot petition?"

He didn't have an answer. He drank the cold tea and looked out at the dining room, where Mr. Chowdhury, who came in every Tuesday for the wonton soup and read the paper for an hour, was watching them over the top of his glasses. Matthew had known him since he was eight, since the year Mr. Chowdhury had helped his father repaint the front of the restaurant after the storm that had been, in Mr. Chowdhury's phrase, capricious, arriving without warning and leaving without apology.

"Señor Chowdhury," Matthew called, because the man spoke four languages and pretended, on principle, to speak only one at a time. "Usted confía en mí?"

Mr. Chowdhury folded the paper with great ceremony. "En usted, en su padre, y en esta sopa," he said. In you, in your father, and in this soup. "Pero si usted me da solamente números, yo me duermo." But if you give me only numbers, I fall asleep.

That was it, Matthew thought, or near it: the numbers were true, the fear was true, and the trust was the bridge between them, and he had been building only the first because the first was easiest to memorize. He turned back to the booth and started again, and this time when the Copenhagen study came up he let his voice drop around it, and when the asthma numbers came he looked at Sally instead of the cards, and once, on purpose, he let a pause run long enough to hurt.

"Better," Sally said when the timer chimed. "You'd almost convinced me." Then she ruined it, cheerfully: "Except that I looked up the Copenhagen thing on the bus, and the drop in admissions they measured was smaller than the margin of error. So your best number might be nothing."

"So argue the other side," Eliott said. "You're allowed to change your mind."

"I can't. The sides are assigned." Matthew gathered the index cards and squared them against the table, thinking that this was the strange part, not the Spanish: that by Friday he would argue, credibly, emotionally, logically, for a position he no longer entirely held, and that the effort of it might be honest anyway, or might not.

Mr. Chowdhury raised his teacup from across the room. "Cinco minutos," he said. "Yo voy a estar escuchando." Five minutes. I will be listening.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Pierre de Coubertin designed the five Olympic rings in 1913, choosing colors so that every national flag of the time contained at least one of them, including the white background.
story:
The big screen had been bolted to scaffolding at one end of the community sports field, and by the time the sun began to drop behind the montane ridge west of town, half the neighborhood had spread blankets across the grass. Kate arrived early with her father, who carried two folding chairs and a cooler, and with Charles-Emile and Jessy trailing behind, arguing already, as they had argued all week, about whether the match actually mattered.

"Of course it matters," Jessy said, dropping onto the grass, which was really more scrub than lawn, the whole field an island of dry grassland biome surrounded by houses. "It's the final. It's the whole country on one pitch."

"It's twenty-two men and a ball," Charles-Emile said. "The country will be exactly the same tomorrow no matter who wins." He said it in his flat, reasonable voice, the one that made Jessy roll her eyes and made Kate feel, guiltily, that he was sometimes right, which was the most annoying thing about him.

The match was still forty minutes away, so the screen showed the opening ceremony footage from earlier in the week, and Kate found herself staring at the Olympic flag while it rippled. Five interlocking rings, blue and yellow and black and green and red, on white. She had looked them up on Tuesday night, after her father said the ceremony might portend good things for the team, and she had gone looking for something else entirely, some sign the universe had arranged itself around her country's fortunes.

"Did you know," she said, and both of them turned, because Kate rarely started sentences that way, "Pierre de Coubertin designed those five rings in 1913?"

"That's the French guy," Mr. Mensah said from behind them. He ran the field, kept the goals netted and the rubbish cleared, and tonight he moved through the blankets selling plastic flags on sticks. "Founder of the modern Olympics. I did a project on him in secondary school. Lost marks because I misspelled his name three different ways."

Kate nodded. "He chose the colors so that every national flag at the time contained at least one of them. Including the white background." She pointed at the screen. "So every country that showed up would see itself somewhere in that flag. Ghana's got the green, the red, the gold, and the white if you count it, which he did." She had not meant to say all of it at once, but it came out in a burst, and she felt strangely exposed, as though she had shown them a page of her diary.

Charles-Emile was quiet for a second, which for him was nearly an apology. "That's actually clever," he admitted. "It's not twenty-two men and a ball, then. It's a flag built out of everyone's flags."

"It's still a design choice," Jessy said. "Some man in a room deciding what would make people feel included."

"It can be both," Kate said. "A man in a room, and it still worked, and it's still working, on us, right now, and I don't think it's wrong to want to feel included." She was thinking of her father, who had watched Ghana's first goal of the tournament with his hands over his mouth like a boy, and who in three weeks was flying out to work in another country, two years, maybe three. He had not said much about it. He was saying even less tonight, sitting slightly apart with his chair angled at the screen, holding one of the little flags Mr. Mensah had given him free.

The match began and the field went loud. Ghana scored in the nineteenth minute and the noise came up off the blankets like something physical, and Kate found herself shouting with Jessy, their arms around each other's shoulders, while Charles-Emile stood unmoving beside them with his hands in his pockets, though she saw that he was smiling. In the second half the other team equalized, and then, in the eighty-fourth minute, scored again off a corner that Kate would replay in her mind for weeks, wondering whether the keeper could have come for it.

When it ended, two to one, nobody left. The crowd thinned slowly, the way it does when losing needs to be carried for a while before anyone can put it down. Mr. Mensah began stacking the plastic flags back into his crate. Kate's father folded his chairs and did not speak, and she stood beside him, not speaking either, watching Charles-Emile argue softly with Jessy about the corner, about the keeper, about whether it would have mattered, and she thought that Coubertin had gotten something right and something wrong at once. Every flag in the rings, every country at the party, and still somebody has to lose, still somebody's father gets on a plane.

She walked over and took one of the little flags out of the crate before Mr. Mensah closed it. He looked at her, then at her father by the scaffolding, and handed her a second one without being asked.

"For him?" she said.

"For both of you," Mr. Mensah said. "The white still counts, you know. Even when you're far away."

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: A counterfactual conditional describes what would have been true if things had been different, such as 'if Sally owned a donkey, she would ride it', and usually implies the 'if' part is false.
story:
David had missed the 7:40 bus by four steps. He had watched its rear doors shudder closed while he was still crossing the parking strip, one shoe untied, and all through first period and into second the sentence kept assembling itself in his head: if he had left five minutes earlier, he would have caught it, and he would not have waited forty minutes in the cold for the next one, and he would not be this tired now. He was still turning the sentence over when he walked into Ms. Jean-Louis's seminar room, where the desks had been pushed into a crooked oval and someone had left a window cracked so that the plastic blind undulated in the draft, clicking softly against the frame.

The topic on the board was "If." Not the word by itself, Ms. Jean-Louis said, dropping a marker into its tray, but the way people use it when they talk about things that did not happen. She wrote an example on the board in her square, careful hand: "If Sally owned a donkey, she would ride it." Then she asked what they noticed, and sat down on the radiator cover as if she had nothing further to add.

Maximilian noticed the donkey first. "Sally doesn't own one," he said. "That's the point of saying it like that. You don't say 'if I own a phone' when you're holding your phone." Jean-Felix, who sat with his chair tipped back at the angle Ms. Jean-Louis pretended not to see, argued that the sentence was really a claim about Sally's character, that it told you she was the kind of person who would ride a donkey if given the chance. The two of them went back and forth, Maximilian insisting the sentence was about the world, Jean-Felix insisting it was about Sally, and David, who usually said nothing in this class, found himself raising his hand before he had decided to.

"I missed my bus this morning," he said, and a few people laughed, which he had expected. "But that's the thing. I keep saying if I'd left five minutes earlier, I would have caught it. And I can't ever check that. It's not like the donkey thing is checkable either, but at least with the donkey you could go buy her one. With the bus, the morning's gone. There's no way to run it again."

"So it's useless," Maximilian said. "It's just complaining with grammar."

"It's not useless," Jean-Felix said, tipping his chair forward with a bang. "You learned something. Leave earlier tomorrow. That's a real lesson, and you got it from the thing that didn't happen."

Ms. Jean-Louis spoke then, only a little. "There's a name for that shape of sentence," she said. "A counterfactual conditional." She wrote the two words under the donkey example, underlined "counter," and went back to the radiator, leaving the room to them.

David copied the words into his notebook and looked at them. Counter to the facts. Conditional. He thought about how his mother talked about her old job, the one in the other city: if she had stayed, they would have made her a manager by now. His father never said anything like that, which David had always taken for stoicism, but maybe it was something else, a refusal to build houses on ground that was not there. He did not think one of them was right and the other wrong. He thought, watching the blind lift and settle in the draft, that Jean-Felix and Maximilian were both partly right, that the sentence told you about the world and about the person at the same time, and that what you did with it depended on which half you needed.

"I think it's both," he said, when Ms. Jean-Louis asked if anyone wanted to answer Maximilian's complaint directly. "The world part is dead, you can't check it, the morning's gone. But the person part is alive. If I'd left earlier, I would have caught it, that tells you the bus was on time and that leaving earlier works. So maybe the rule is you only get to say it if you'd act on it. Otherwise it's just weather, you know, capricious, it just happens to you."

"Everything just happens to you," Maximilian said. "That's what happening is."

"No," Jean-Felix said, and started to say more, and stopped, because the bell had not rung yet and he wanted to get it right. Ms. Jean-Louis was smiling faintly at the window, not helping either of them. David drew a small donkey in the margin of his notes, beside the two underlined words, and wrote underneath it, in pencil, light enough to erase: maybe. The blind clicked against the frame once more, and the bell rang, and Maximilian was still talking as they all stood up.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: The Quran, in Surah 2, Al-Baqarah, exempts people who are ill or travelling from fasting during Ramadan, directing them to make up the same number of days later.
story:
The cemetery gate was still open when Aiden got there, which surprised him, because in his mind it had always been closed, the way places are in memories you haven't visited in three years. He had come to see his grandfather's grave before the debate tournament and before Ramadan overlapped with the trip, though he couldn't have said which errand mattered more. His uncle was already standing at the headstone, hat in his hands, looking less like a man grieving than like a stoic waiting for a bus, which was exactly how his grandfather had looked at funerals, and probably how Aiden would look someday too.

"You brought the thing?" his uncle asked, without turning around.

Aiden held up his phone. On it was the text Mr. Bakker had assigned for the debate unit: read the primary source itself, argue from the text, no shortcuts through commentary. The resolution was whether an ancient religious rule still applied in modern life, and Aiden had drawn the Ramadan fast. He had also, less officially, drawn a problem. The tournament fell inside the fast, two hundred miles away, and he was not sure a person could argue for nine hours on no water.

They sat on the low stone wall near the grave, and his uncle took the phone and scrolled with one thumb, squinting. "You know this section?" he said. "Surah two. Al-Baqarah. Your grandfather could recite the whole thing, but I only ever got partway." He turned the screen back toward Aiden and pointed at a line as if it were a name on a map.

Aiden read it twice. The verse exempted people who were ill or travelling from fasting during Ramadan, directing them to make up the same number of days later. He looked up, then back down, as if the words might rearrange themselves. "It just says that? Right there?"

"Right there," his uncle said. "You seem disappointed."

"No, it's..." Aiden turned the phone off and on again, a habit he'd developed when a fact seemed too convenient to be real. He had spent a week dreading a choice between looking devout and feeling dizzy, and the choice, apparently, had been made in the text fourteen centuries before he was born. But that was what bothered him. If the rule contained its own exceptions, then what exactly was he supposed to debate?

He texted Dwayne, who had drawn the opposing side and had been annoyingly confident about it all week. The message scene unfolded on the small screen while his uncle prayed quietly a few feet away, palms open on his knees.

So the text literally gives travelers a pass, Aiden typed. What's your argument now, that airlines didn't exist back then?

Dwayne's reply came fast, in three bubbles. My argument is that's not an exemption, it's a deferment. Same number of days later, it says. You still owe the days. So the rule applies in modern life exactly as hard as it always did, it just schedules around you.

Aiden stared at that for a long moment. It was better than he wanted it to be. He typed, deleted, typed again. Then his uncle, finishing the prayer, leaned over and read the exchange over his shoulder, which Aiden pretended not to mind.

"He's got you," his uncle said, almost cheerful. "You're looking for the text to be either a cage or a door, and it's being neither. It's being practical." He tapped the headstone with one knuckle, gently. "Your grandfather fasted through a cholera summer when he was fourteen because he thought hardship was the point. I always thought he was trying to subjugate the body to prove something to himself. He would have hated this verse, I think. Or loved it and ignored it."

That was the thing Aiden hadn't expected to learn in a cemetery: that the same text could make a rule lighter and heavier at once. He walked the rows while his uncle stayed with the grave, reading other names, other dates, noticing how the old stones were all in one language and the new ones in two, and how the oldest families had been buried here so long the ground itself seemed to belong to them, autochthonous as the granite, though of course nobody was, really. Everyone had come from somewhere, even the dead. He filed the word away for the debate, where it might do some work.

In the car going back, he asked his uncle what he actually thought. Was a traveller's exemption a weakening of the rule or a strengthening of it? Did mercy make a law more binding, because you trusted it more, or less, because it bent?

His uncle took a while, the way he did with questions he considered real. "I think a rule that can't survive a journey isn't much of a rule," he said finally. "But you should argue it, not me. You're the one on the team." Then, at the red light, he added, "So what will you do? At the tournament. Eat or fast?"

Aiden looked out the window at the strip mall sliding past, the same one that had been there when his grandfather drove this road. "Make up the days later," he said. "Same number. It's in the text." He was honest enough, with himself anyway, to admit the decision felt both like obedience and like relief, and that he couldn't separate the two, and that maybe for the debate he didn't have to.

"And the arguing?" his uncle said, pulling away from the light. "Which side are you taking?"

"The one where I say the rule applies, exactly as written," Aiden said, "and that Dwayne is right that it applies harder than people think." He pulled out his phone and started typing the first note for his case.

"Good," his uncle said. "Text him that. Word for word."

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: Tennessee Williams called The Glass Menagerie, first staged in Chicago in 1944, a memory play: it is narrated by Tom, who looks back on his family.
story:
Ms. Clarke had taped the assignment sheet to the blackboard weeks ago, but Taylor only read it properly on the morning the drafts were due: a ten-minute play, staged in the studio theatre, drawn from a moment in the playwright's own life. She had a notebook full of half-scenes and nothing she was willing to say out loud.

She found Olive at the lunch table by the window, tearing the crust off a sandwich. "Do you have your moment yet?" Taylor asked, and Olive said she was writing about the summer her grandmother taught her to swim, that it was easy, that the water did the work for her. Taylor turned her pen over and over on the table. "Everything true that happened to me is either boring or not mine to tell," she said. Olive looked at her the way she looked at crossword clues, patient, waiting for the answer to admit itself.

After last period, Taylor went to the library and pulled down the play anthology Ms. Clarke had left on the reserve shelf. Nicolas was already there, elbows on the table, a script open in front of him with lines highlighted in three colours. "I'm stealing from the best," he said without looking up. "What are you doing?" She showed him her blank notebook, and he slid the anthology across. "Read the intro to this one. It's about a family, but the brother tells it from later, like he's remembering at us."

Taylor read the introduction twice. The Glass Menagerie, first staged in Chicago in 1944, and Tennessee Williams had called it a memory play, narrated by Tom, who looks back on his family. She copied the phrase onto her palm in ballpoint. "Memory play," she said out loud, and Nicolas nodded and took the book back.

That was the heuristic she had been missing, though she wouldn't have used that word until Ms. Clarke's quiz on Friday. Taylor didn't have to put her mother onstage and pretend to be her. She could stand at the edge of the stage herself and speak from two years away, telling the audience what the kitchen smelled like the night her father's boxes went out to the car, while two actors played it out in the light behind her. The distance was the point. In the car on the way home, her mother had tried to inculcate a kind of cheerfulness, saying the apartment would be easier to clean, and Taylor had believed her for almost a year.

She wrote the whole draft that evening at the kitchen counter, the dishwasher hissing, the notebook paper curling under her wrist. At rehearsal on Thursday she cast Olive as the mother and Nicolas as the father with no lines, only the boxes. Taylor stood in the wings and delivered the narration into the dark. Ms. Clarke watched from the third row with her coat still on, and when it ended she said the narrator's speeches were incisive, that they cut to the marrow, then asked one question: "Whose memory is this, yours or your mother's?"

Taylor had assumed the answer was obvious. But during the second run-through she watched Olive say the line about the apartment being easier to clean, and she heard, for the first time, how tired the voice behind it might have been. The narrator Taylor had written knew everything, judged everything, hovered like a judge over her mother's shoulder, and it struck her that the play was not memory but verdict. She stopped the rehearsal. "I've been directing it wrong," she said. "I'm not looking back at my family. I'm looking down at it." Olive lowered the dish towel prop and Nicolas set down his box.

They ran it again with one change, a small one. When Olive spoke, Taylor let the narration fall silent for eight full seconds, and the audience, she hoped, would not know whose silence it was. There was a twist she kept for herself as well: at the very end, the narrator admitted she did not remember the colour of the moving truck, only that it rained, only that her father waved with one glove on and one glove lost, and that her mother made pancakes the next morning as if pancakes were an argument nobody had to win. Whether that was the truth or the story she had built over it, she could not say, and the play did not say either.

On the night of the performance, the studio theatre smelled of dust and radiator heat, and forty chairs held maybe twenty people. Taylor stood in the dark at the edge of the light, and behind her Olive picked up a plate that was not there and turned it over slowly, twice.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The word diploma comes from a Greek word meaning "paper folded double," from the earlier practice of folding official documents.
story:
The envelope from State arrived on a Tuesday, and Henry carried it to the kitchen table without opening it, the way his mother had taught him to carry things that mattered. She put down her coffee. His grandfather's camera sat on the counter, sent two weeks ago with a note that said only, for the graduate. Inside the envelope was the bill for orientation, four hundred dollars, due by June first, and neither of them said anything about the checking account for a long moment.

"We'll figure it out," his mother said, which was what she always said, and Henry had begun to hear it as its own kind of information, a measure of how bad the number was.

He had a job, eight hours a week at the garden center, but the math was blunt. Two hundred and forty a month, minus gas, minus the fifty he owed Haydn for the prom tickets he'd insisted on splitting. He could ask Mr. Otieno, his old English teacher, who had offered once in the hallway to write a reference for anything Henry needed, but a reference didn't pay a deposit.

The graduation rehearsal was Thursday morning in the gym. Amelie saved him a seat and spent the whole hour complaining, in a low voice, about the principal's elocution, mimicking the way he swallowed the ends of his sentences until even the word congratulations came out as something like congralations. Henry laughed, and then didn't, because he was calculating, again, the four hundred, and Amelie noticed. She always noticed.

"You're doing the thing," she said. "The thing where you go somewhere else."

"Orientation deposit," he said. "It's due before I get paid again."

"My dad could lend it," Amelie said, and Henry said no before she finished, and she shrugged like she'd expected that. He wasn't proud of the no. It had come out faster than thinking.

That afternoon he found his father in the garage, sorting screws into jars, which his father did when he wanted to seem busy. Henry stood in the doorway with the bill folded in his pocket. His father worked maintenance at the hospital and had been on the night shift since March, and they had been conducting their whole relationship in eleven-minute increments in the driveway. Henry had already decided, in a vague and unexamined way, that he wouldn't ask. His father had paid for the first year of his own college and then run out of money and never gone back, and there was a version of Henry's plan that involved never being that person, never needing the rescue.

He asked anyway. He pulled out the bill and said the number out loud, and his father set down the jar of screws and looked at the paper for longer than reading could take. "I can cover half by Friday," his father said. "Haydn's dad is buying the camera equipment off me, the old lenses, so there's some room." Henry hadn't known his father still had the old lenses, or that Haydn's dad would want them. It rearranged something. The refusal he'd been rehearsing, the self-sufficiency of it, suddenly looked less like a principle and more like a pose.

Saturday was the ceremony itself. The gym smelled like floor wax and cut lilies, and Mr. Otieno found Henry in the line outside, straightened his collar without comment, and said, "Diploma comes from a Greek word meaning paper folded double. From when they folded official documents in half." Henry had assumed the man would say something about the future. He said only that, and moved down the line.

When Henry crossed the stage and took the folder, it was lighter than he expected. He sat down between Amelie and a boy from his chemistry class and opened it on his knee. The paper inside lay flat, unfolded, its seal pressed into the leatherette on one side. He showed it to Amelie.

"It's not even folded," he whispered. "Etymologically false advertising." She snorted into her hand, and the boy from chemistry leaned over to look, and for a second the three of them were bent around the thing, this single sheet, doing the work of two.

His mother was waiting afterward near the doors with her phone raised, and behind her his father stood in his work clothes, having driven straight from the shift, holding a plastic bag with the camera in it. Henry walked toward them with the folder under his arm and the bill already half paid in his mind, the other half certain now in a way it hadn't been on Tuesday, and he was still deciding whether to tell his father the joke about the Greek or save it for the car.

"Smile," his mother said, and he did, and behind her his father raised the bag and shook it once, like a bell.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Hydroplaning happens when a layer of water builds up between the tires and the road so the car loses traction; easing off the accelerator can let the tires regain grip.
story:
The parking lot behind the shuttered grocery store had the gray, puddled look of a place that had given up on commerce, which was exactly why Mr. Dhillon liked it for first lessons. Jason slid into the driver's seat, adjusted the mirror three times to postpone the inevitable, and put both hands on the wheel as if it were a sleeping animal he didn't want to wake. Alina climbed into the back with her chin on the front seat, having invited herself along on the grounds that she wanted to witness history.

"Clutch, brake, key," Mr. Dhillon said from the passenger side, in the tone of a man reciting a prayer he'd said four hundred times. Jason had spent the week reading the manual cover to cover, mostly to disabuse his father of the idea that he'd inherited the family talent for stalling. His father had stalled a car at his own wedding, a story told at every Thanksgiving with tremendous pride, as though it were an athletic achievement.

The engine caught on the first try. "Miracle," Alina said, and clapped twice, solemnly, like a seal at a graduation.

They spent twenty minutes on the basics, the car lurching and settling across the painted lines while the rain thickened against the windshield. Mr. Dhillon had the wipers on intermittent, which produced a somnolence in Jason that he fought off by narrating everything out loud, "releasing brake, creeping forward, still alive," until Alina threatened to charge him admission. The lot had a low stretch near the storm drain where the water had pooled into a wide, turgid sheet, brownish at the edges and smooth in the middle, like a table someone had varnished badly.

"Go through it," Mr. Dhillon said. "Slow."

Jason was not slow. He was seventeen and the accelerator was a new and fascinating invention, and the car hit the water at a speed the manual would have called inadvisable. The steering went light under his hands. Not stiff, not resistant, just suddenly, horribly weightless, as if the wheel had been disconnected and reconnected to nothing. The car drifted left without asking him. Alina stopped joking, which was how he knew it was serious.

His first instinct was to brake, and his foot was already moving, but something surfaced from page ninety-three of the manual, read at one in the morning: hydroplaning happens when a layer of water builds up between the tires and the road, so the car loses traction. Braking would do nothing for tires that weren't touching anything. The book's advice had been oddly gentle. Ease off the accelerator. Let the tires find the road again. It had seemed too simple at one in the morning, a remedy for a problem described in physics, and now it seemed like the only sentence in the world. He took his foot off the gas and held the wheel where it was, doing nothing on purpose, which was the hardest thing he had ever done with his whole leg.

The engine noise dropped. The car slowed itself, unglamorously, and then the steering came back under his palms, heavy and ordinary and real, and the tires bit the wet asphalt with a sound like a zipper closing. He steered out of the drift and rolled to a stop in the middle of the lot with his heart performing percussion. "That," he said, "was hydroplaning. That's what that's called." Alina exhaled from the back seat. "You said it like a weatherman. Do it again but calmer."

Mr. Dhillon was quiet for a moment, which Jason had learned to distrust. "The book told you to ease off," he said finally. It wasn't a question.

"I read it. I didn't believe it would work." Jason turned the car in a slow circle through the shallower water, feeling the wheel's new weight in his wrists, deciding he wasn't sure whether what he'd done was courage or arithmetic, and whether those were different things, and whether he cared. He circled the puddle a second time at a crawl, then a third at a careful speed, tires hissing and holding. Alina leaned between the seats and pointed at the drain. "Flood that whole thing and open a water park," she said. "I'll run the gift shop."

"Back through it once more," said Mr. Dhillon, and settled into his seat. "Slowly, this time." Jason checked the mirror, signaled out of habit into the empty lot, and drove straight at the water.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: The STAR method structures an interview answer as Situation, Task, Action and Result, so a story about past experience ends with what actually happened.
story:
The birthday party was in Charles's backyard, and Jake had been practicing his handshake on the kitchen doorframe when Jaxson found him.

"You're doing it here?" Jaxson asked. "The interview's Monday."

"That's the point." Jake wiped his palms on his jeans. "I need an audience or I fall apart."

Charles's little brother shrieked past with a water gun. Somewhere near the fence, Mr. Campbell, who taught junior business and had come over with a casserole dish, was arguing amiably with Charles's father about the grill. Jake had his notebook out, though, pages of crossed-out answers, because the bakery on Miller Road was hiring and he wanted that counter job more than he had wanted anything he could name.

"Sit," Jake said, pointing at a lawn chair. "Be the manager."

Jaxson lounged into the chair, dour all of a sudden, arms folded. "Fine. Why do you want to work here?"

Jake opened his mouth and nothing organized came out. He wanted the money for the fall, he liked the smell of bread, his mother had said he should stop being so vague, he was good with people except when he wasn't. The sentences collided and he heard himself trailing into "and, um, other stuff," and Jaxson's eyebrows rose a millimeter, which was worse than laughing.

"You talked for two minutes," Jaxson said. "I don't remember anything except the bread."

"I panicked. Ask me about experience."

"Tell me about a time you handled a difficult customer."

Jake had an answer. He'd covered the concession stand at the swim meet when a woman insisted the register had shortchanged her, and he'd stayed calm, mostly, and counted the drawer twice, and it had turned out she'd miscounted her change, and he'd been polite about it. But when he tried to tell it, he began with the weather, detoured through his inability to work the hot dog roller, and never actually got to what had happened at the end. Jaxson interrupted to take a call from someone at the party, and Jake understood that the story had died before its ending, again.

He walked over to the drink table, mostly to stop talking. Mr. Campbell was there filling a cup, and Jake, without planning to, asked him whether interviews were really as bad as they felt.

"Depends on the shape of your answers," Mr. Campbell said. "Ask Charles. He did a whole project on it last spring."

Charles, cake knife in hand, grinned. "STAR method. Situation, Task, Action, Result. You structure each answer that way, so a story about your past experience ends with what actually happened."

"So it doesn't just trail off."

"It can't trail off. The Result is the whole point." Charles was called away to candles then, and that was all the instruction Jake got, which somehow made it easier to hold.

Back at the lawn chair, Jake tried again, and the difference surprised him. Situation: the concession stand, the meet, the angry woman. Task: resolve it without a manager present. Action: counted the drawer twice, offered to recount her change with her, kept his voice level. Result: she found the missing dollar in her own pocket, apologized, and bought a lemonade on the way out. Ninety seconds. Jaxson actually nodded.

"That was a real answer," Jaxson said. "Do the handshake again. You're doing this weird thing where you look at my chin."

They ran it three more times while the party moved toward cake and someone's speaker died and had to be resuscitated by Charles's father, who shook the auxiliary cord like a man defibrillating a patient. Between rounds, Jake caught himself weighing the method itself. It felt honest, because the Result had to be true or the whole story collapsed, and it felt like a trick, because no actual conversation with another human being ran in four tidy segments. He couldn't decide whether he was learning to communicate or learning to package himself, and he said so.

"Both," Jaxson said. "So what. The bakery doesn't want your soul. They want to know you won't freeze when the drawer's off by ten dollars."

"That's the apportionment I'm not sure about," Jake said. "How much of it is me and how much is performance."

Jaxson shrugged. "Ask her Monday."

The candles were lit and the little kids were assembling around the table, and Jake stood at the edge of that, notebook closed in his back pocket, running the STAR shape one more time in his head, Situation, Task, Action, Result, like a handrail he could choose to hold or not. Charles waved him over to help with the cake.

"Big slice for the employed," Charles called, "and for the about-to-be."

"Monday," Jake said, and went to cut cake.

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: Philosopher Stephen Toulmin, in his 1958 book The Uses of Argument, described an argument's backbone as a claim, the grounds or data supporting it, and a warrant explaining why those grounds support the claim.
story:
At six-thirty Anthony sat down to pasta and his phone lit up on the table, screen up, which his mother had a rule about. He turned it face down and cut his noodles. His father asked how the physics test had gone and Anthony said probably fine, which was the answer that ended questions, and it did. The phone buzzed twice against the wood. A small knocking sound, like a knuckle on a door.

It was Kenza. Her messages came in bursts, three at a time, always out of order. She was writing a persuasive essay for Ms. Ferreira, due tomorrow, about banning plastic water bottles on campus. Her first message said the draft was done. Her second said Ms. Ferreira had read the rough copy and written one comment in red at the top. Her third was a photo of the comment.

"Your evidence is solid," Anthony read aloud, tilting the screen so only he could see it, though his mother noticed anyway. "But you never show me why the evidence proves your point."

"That's the whole paper," his father said, when Anthony explained, mostly to his plate. "Sounds like she's saying it's fine."

"She said it's fine and broken at the same time." Anthony scrolled down through the photo of the draft. Kenza had six paragraphs. She had a survey of three hundred students, a number from the custodian about how many bottles the recycling bins overflowed with each week, a quote from somebody about microplastics. It was, in its way, profligate with evidence; she had gathered more than any reasonable essay needed. And Ms. Ferreira's comment sat above all of it like a roof over a house with no walls.

His mother took a bite of salad and said that in her day you wrote five paragraphs and handed it in. Anthony said that in her day nobody texted you a photo of the teacher's handwriting at dinner, and she conceded the point. His father asked what the actual problem was, since the evidence was, apparently, solid.

"That's what I'm trying to figure out." He carried his plate to the counter, took his phone, and went down the hall to his room, where his debate binder lived on the shelf between the AP US History binder and a box of dead mechanical pencils. He had a photocopied page in one of the dividers from when he'd started debate club sophomore year before quitting, a page Ms. Ferreira had handed out to the whole team. He found it. Toulmin. A philosopher named Stephen Toulmin, in a 1958 book called The Uses of Argument, had described the backbone of an argument as three parts: a claim, the grounds or data supporting it, and a warrant. Anthony had underlined "warrant" back then because he'd liked the sound of it and never thought about it since. The warrant, the sheet said, was the part explaining why the grounds support the claim. The bridge. Not the pillars, not the far bank. The bridge.

He typed to Kenza: What's your claim? She answered: The school should ban plastic water bottles. He typed: And your evidence? She listed the survey, the custodian's count, the microplastics quote. He sat on the floor with the binder open on his knees and tried to make it work like the sheet said. Claim: ban the bottles. Grounds: three hundred students say they'd support it, the bins overflow, microplastics exist somewhere in the world. The warrant had to say why those grounds, specifically, made the claim true. Three hundred students support it, so the ban would succeed, so we should do it. Except that was a new argument, not a bridge, and it depended on a condition. If the school actually enforced it. If the fountain water was drinkable, which, Anthony knew from the gym hallway, it was not.

Kenza sent a string of question marks. He called her.

"Okay," he said. "You have a claim. You have grounds. The thing Ms. Ferreira wants is the warrant. That's the word, warrant. The line that says why your evidence supports your claim."

"You mean like a topic sentence?"

"No, a topic sentence is just the capsule. This is the logic inside it." He heard his own voice doing the thing debate kids did, and he dialed it back. "Look at your survey paragraph. You say three hundred students support a ban. Then you jump straight to therefore ban it. But the survey only holds if banning actually changes anything, and your custodian's count says the bottles are already going somewhere, so where do they go after the ban?"

"The bins, if we build better bins."

"Then your essay isn't about banning bottles. It's about infrastructure, and your survey supports a different claim than the one on your title page."

There was a silence on the line that he took for either thinking or offence. He lay back on the rug and stared at the ceiling, where a glow star from middle school still hung, half peeled. He thought about telling her to keep the ban claim and find better grounds, and then thought that the survey was genuinely good, the best thing in the paper, and that maybe the claim should move to meet the evidence instead. Both directions were possible. He said so. He said he didn't know which one was right, that Toulmin's sheet told you what the parts were but not which part to sacrifice when they didn't line up.

"So what do I do?"

"What do you actually believe? Forget the essay. If they ban the bottles tomorrow and the fountains still taste like pennies, is that a win?"

Kenza didn't answer right away. Down the hall his mother called that there was garlic bread if he wanted it, and he said in a minute, and Kenza said, "Hold on, I'm writing something," and he could hear her typing on the other end, fast, the way she did when she'd stopped asking and started deciding.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: On level ground with no air resistance, a launch angle of 45 degrees gives the greatest range for a given launch speed.
story:
Victoria sat at the kitchen table with the textbook open to chapter three and a bag of frozen peas pressed against her forehead. The peas were meant to assuage the headache that had arrived somewhere between the third practice problem and the fifth, though mostly they made her glasses fog. On the page, a diagram showed a ball leaving a cliff at an angle, with two arrows sprouting from it: one flat along the ground, one straight up. The caption said the arrows were the horizontal and vertical components of the velocity, and that they could be treated separately. Victoria had read this four times.

Her mother passed through with a laundry basket and stopped long enough to read over her shoulder. "When I was your age we didn't split anything," she said. "We just threw things." She went on toward the basement, and Victoria turned back to problem six, which asked how far a stone would travel if launched at fourteen meters per second at an angle of thirty degrees.

She did what the book said. She drew the arrows. She multiplied fourteen by the cosine of thirty for the flat arrow, fourteen by the sine of thirty for the upright one, and wrote the two numbers side by side as if they belonged to two different stones. The vertical stone rose, slowed, stopped, fell, and hit the ground after a certain number of seconds. The horizontal stone, meanwhile, sailed along at a steady rate, not caring about the fall at all, and covered ground the whole time the first stone was in the air. She multiplied the flat speed by the time in the air and got a distance. Then she checked the answer in the back and found she was off by a factor of ten, which turned out to be a decimal point she had dropped in line two.

Her phone buzzed on the table. It was a message from Loic, sent from his kitchen two streets over, where the science fair team had gathered around the ball launcher they had built from PVC pipe and a garage door spring.

"Emergency," the message read. "Contest is who launches a ball the farthest across the gym floor. Maximilian has the angle set at 30 because he says low and fast wins. Ms. Do wouldn't tell us anything, she just smiled and said we should test it. We have until Saturday. Come over?"

Victoria looked at problem six, at her two stones, at the answer now correct in the back of the book. She typed back that she'd come after dinner, and then, because something in the diagram was bothering her, she stayed at the table instead of starting the dishes.

She made a column on the back of her history notes. For the same launch speed, the one given in the problem, she tried thirty degrees and worked out the range. Then forty. Then fifty. The numbers came out of the same two-step routine every time: the vertical component decided how long the ball stayed in the air, the horizontal component decided how fast it covered ground while aloft, and the range was the product. At thirty degrees the ball flew fast but briefly. At sixty it lingered but crawled. She noticed, without deciding to notice, that thirty and sixty gave the same range, which felt like a symmetry she couldn't quite account for, and that somewhere between them the numbers peaked. She tried forty-four. Then forty-five. Then forty-six. The peak sat at forty-five exactly, on level ground, if you ignored the air.

She carried the page across the street to her own front yard and threw a tennis ball at a low angle, then a high one, then something in between, and the in-between throw went farther, though the yard was short and the porch light was bad and the tennis ball was not a physics ball. It was evidence, but thin evidence. She wrote the numbers down anyway.

At Loic's kitchen the next afternoon, the launcher lay across two chairs with its spring exposed and its barrel angle set by a protractor taped to the pivot. Maximilian was leaning against the counter repeating his argument, which had begun to sound like oratory, complete with a raised finger and a pause for effect: that speed was what mattered and that a low angle kept the ball moving fast. Ms. Do had left a plate of clementines on the counter before withdrawing to the living room, in the manner of a person who intended to hear the results but not to cause them.

Victoria put her history notes on the table and turned them toward the others. She said that on level ground with no air resistance, an angle of forty-five degrees gave the greatest range for a given launch speed. She said the vertical part of the launch and the horizontal part could be worked separately, and that at forty-five they balanced. Maximilian asked what happened off a cliff or in the wind, and she said she didn't know yet, that her page only covered flat ground and still air, and that the gym floor was flat and the gym was probably still.

Loic had already found masking tape. They marked a starting line on the kitchen floor, which was tile, not wood, and laid a tape measure along it toward the back door, and fired a practice ball at thirty degrees. It struck the pantry door. At forty-five it sailed past the coat rack and rolled to the base of the washing machine. They measured both. Maximilian demanded a third trial at thirty, and it lost again, and he demanded a fourth, and it lost by more. He sat down on the floor next to the tape measure and began peeling a clementine without looking up.

From the living room Ms. Do said, without coming in, "You'll want to check that it holds at a different spring setting." Loic looked at Victoria. Victoria looked at the protractor taped to the pivot, which had slipped a little during the trials, so that the angle they had called forty-five might have been forty-three, or forty-seven, or something in between. She picked up the protractor, pressed the tape flat with her thumb, and set the barrel by hand to the line.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: Japan has one of the world's oldest populations, with about 29 percent of its people aged 65 or over in the early 2020s.
story:
The Honda's air conditioning had died somewhere outside Reno, which was why Jesse was reading a printout about Japan with the windows down and highway grit settling on his teeth. Anika was driving him to San Francisco for his flight, a five-hour favor she had announced as "two hours of conversation and three of you shutting up while I sing." He had the exchange program packet in his lap, and stapled to the back of it, for reasons known only to Mr. Becker, was a worksheet on population pyramids.

"Becker's making me do homework before I even land," Jesse said. He held up the page, which showed two bar charts shaped like Christmas trees lying on their sides. "Apparently I'm supposed to analyze this and predict whether they need more schools or nursing homes."

"Predict it for who?"

"For Japan. That's where I'm going." He squinted at the chart. "It says about 29 percent of the people there are 65 or over. Early 2020s. That's almost a third of the country."

Anika changed lanes without signaling, which she did whenever a semicolon of moral importance arrived in her thinking. "So more nursing homes, obviously. That's the answer. Write it in the margin and let's get boba in Truckee."

"It's not obviously anything. That's the whole point of the worksheet." He turned the pyramid sideways, as if gravity might redistribute the population. Young bars stacked thick in the middle, thin at the bottom. Elderly bars heavy at the top. "Look, if the bottom is skinny, fewer kids are coming up behind. But the middle is still fat.
