So right now there are lots of workers, and lots of old people, and few children. Which means what, in like ten years?"

"That the workers become the old people and nobody replaces them." She said it the way she said most true things, slightly annoyed to be the one holding them. "Which is what the shape already told you. The pyramid isn't a pyramid, Jesse. It's a lightbulb."

He laughed despite the grit. It did look like a lightbulb. The worksheet wanted him to write a paragraph, and the paragraph, he suspected, was supposed to be confident. Predict: schools or nursing homes. Choose one. Mr. Becker had a note in red pen at the top, Be specific, which was Becker's way of saying be brave, which was Becker's way of saying anything at all.

They stopped in Truckee for gas and the drink Anika had promised herself. Inside, Jesse watched a cashier help an old man count out coins with a patience that seemed to belong to another economy of time. Behind them a toddler screamed about a bag of cheddar bunnies with the full force of her volition. Jesse caught himself doing the arithmetic without meaning to. One of them, then the other. A country was just this, multiplied. He texted Elianna, who was doing a gap year and claimed to know things: if a quarter plus of a country is over 65, do you build schools or nursing homes?

Her reply arrived as he was buckling back in. wrong question. you build neither, you argue about trains and hospitals and who does the care work. also tell Anika she owes me $12.

"Your friend is an idiot," Jesse reported.

"My friend is right, though. That's the exhausting thing about her."

The road past Donner Lake went on interminably, sun off the water like a held note. Jesse worked the problem from both ends, which was the only method Mr. Becker had ever endorsed. From the top down: more elderly meant more care, more clinics, more homes, more hands. From the bottom up: fewer children meant closing schools, which meant teachers doing something else, which meant the whole ladder of jobs reshuffling. And yet the two perspectives refused to merge into a single prediction. The shape told him what a country had been; it argued about what the country would become. He could say more nursing homes with a fat asterisk, or he could say it depends and feel like a coward.

Somewhere before Sacramento he wrote his answer in the margin of the worksheet, small, as if it might get him in trouble: "More elder care, probably. Schools for the ones still coming, just fewer. Uncertain: timing, and who pays." Then he interposed the pen between his teeth and stared at the lightbulb-shaped chart until Anika told him to stop chewing his instruments.

At the terminal she hugged him too briefly for sentiment and said, "Text me the pyramid of wherever you land." The security line folded him into its gray procession, and at the gate he found a seat beside an elderly couple speaking Japanese, the woman's hand resting on the man's sleeve, both of them watching the board with the patience he had seen at the gas station. Jesse took out the worksheet one more time and drew a small arrow from the man's approximate position on the pyramid toward the future, then looked up when they called his row.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, set up in 1988 by the World Meteorological Organization and the UN Environment Programme, does no original research; it assesses the published scientific literature.
story:
The gym smelled of vinegar and overheated glue guns, which Aiden took as a good sign, since his own project depended on both. His display board, "Reading the Ocean's Diary," compared three published studies on coral bleaching thresholds, and beside it he had wired a tank whose water heated one degree per hour while a probe logged everything to a laptop with a cracked screen. He wanted the regional prize, which came with two hundred dollars and a lab tour, but mostly he wanted Ms. Rossi to stop describing his work as "ambitious" in that particular tone she reserved for half-finished things.

Arlo arrived at the neighboring table carrying a hand-painted globe and a stack of printouts an inch thick. His board said, in letters visible from the parking lot, "The IPCC Says the Oceans Are Dying." He propped the globe on a stack of textbooks like a witness taking the stand.

"Yours is three papers," Arlo said, leaning over Aiden's table. "Mine is the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. Thousands of scientists. They run all the biggest climate experiments on Earth. It's not even close."

Aiden had assumed something like that too, once. But during his reading he'd kept landing on the same strange detail, and he wasn't sure he'd understood it, so he didn't say anything yet. He tightened the clamp on his heating element and said, "Judges come through at ten."

The judges came through at ten. The first one, a man with a lanyard and a pen he never used, spent four minutes at Arlo's table. Aiden caught only fragments from across the aisle, but one fragment was Arlo saying, clearly and with total confidence, "The IPCC measures it directly, their own instruments, their own ships." The judge nodded and wrote nothing.

When the man reached Aiden's table, he looked at the tank, then at the graph from Study Two, which didn't match the graph from Study One, and asked the question Aiden had been dreading. "So which one is right?"

"That's kind of the point," Aiden said. "Study Two couldn't replicate the first team's numbers. They used different reef sites. So a third group went back and did it again, and landed in between." He tapped the middle graph. "Nobody's declared a winner. They're still arguing in the letters section."

The judge made a small noise, not displeased, and moved on. Gabryel, who was wandering the fair with a cup of punch and no project of his own, drifted over and lowered her voice. "Arlo's telling everyone the IPCC has its own fleet of research vessels. He told the freshman from the robotics club it has submarines."

"He doesn't know," Aiden said. "I didn't either until Tuesday." He pulled up the IPCC's own website on the laptop, careful to angle the cracked screen away from the tank's splash zone. "Look. It says it right here. The IPCC was set up in 1988 by the World Meteorological Organization and the UN Environment Programme." He scrolled. "And it does no original research. It assesses the published scientific literature. That's all it does. It reads what everyone else has already published and puts it together."

"Wait." Gabryel squinted. "So it's like a giant group project where nobody does the experiment?"

"It's like if you took every study ever done on coral and wrote one enormous report on what they all agree about," Aiden said. "Which is actually harder to argue with. Or should be."

The word had gotten around by lunch, as words do, and the gym's low ferment of gossip settled into something more watchful. Arlo came to Aiden's table with his globe under one arm like a confiscated soccer ball. "You told Gabryel my board is wrong."

"Your board's title is fine," Aiden said. "The part where you said they run their own experiments isn't. They don't. They never have. They assess the literature."

Arlo stood there long enough that the heating element clicked off behind them, a small mechanical sigh. "Then why does everyone cite them like they're the ultimate source?"

"Because they read everything," Aiden said. "That's the ultimate source part." He hesitated, because the honest answer had a hole in it. "I think. I mean, I still don't fully get how they weigh papers that disagree, or what happens when a whole field is wrong. That part I couldn't figure out."

Ms. Rossi passed behind them carrying a clipboard and a plate of celery nobody would eat, and paused. "Truce, gentlemen?"

"Detente," Arlo said, surprising everyone including himself, and set the globe down on the corner of Aiden's table. The two boards stood there side by side, his and Aiden's, the inch of printouts next to the three stubborn graphs that refused to match.

The judges returned at two. The man with the unused pen stopped between the tables, looked at the coral graphs, then at the globe, and said, "So tell me how you two would know if you were both wrong." The friable edge of Aiden's display board chose that moment to shed a curl of cardboard onto the floor, and both of them bent to pick it up, and neither of them answered first.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In a presidential system, the president is elected separately from the legislature for a fixed term and cannot be removed simply because the legislature disagrees with them.
story:
The courthouse smelled of floor wax and old paper, and Edouard had been sitting on its wooden bench for forty minutes, which was long enough to learn that the building had its own biome: recycled air, fluorescent light, a slow river of people moving between doors that opened and shut with hydraulic sighs. He kept his summons folded into quarters in his back pocket, though he had already memorized what it said. Witness, Room 4C, ten o'clock. It was now ten past eleven.

He was not alone. Bronson had come with him, which surprised him, since Bronson usually treated civic obligations the way other people treated dentist appointments. And Sirine was there because her civics class had been assigned to observe a morning of small claims, though she had finished observing within the first hour and now sat between them, eating sunflower seeds from a paper cone.

"You can't eat those in a courthouse," Edouard said.

"Watch me," said Sirine, but she folded the cone shut and put it in her bag, which was her way of conceding a point while pretending not to.

Bronson had his phone out, scrolling through news from home, and every few minutes he made a sound of disgust. Finally he turned the screen around. "They're trying to remove our president again. Third time in two years. It's a circus."

"That's because your system is broken," Sirine said.

"It is not broken. It's presidential. We elect the president separately from the legislature, for a fixed term. He serves that term whether they like him or not. Congress can't remove him just because they disagree with him."

Sirine cracked a seed against her teeth, slow and deliberate. "Where I'm from, the parliament picks the prime minister. She sits in parliament. If she loses the chamber, she's out the same week. My father calls it a dignity, not a weakness. The government falls, nobody's head rolls."

"That's absurd," Bronson said. "You could have a new head of government every month."

"We don't. But we could. That's the point. The majority rules or it doesn't."

Edouard had been half listening, the way you half listen when your own morning is coiled tight inside you. But something in the argument caught, the way a sleeve catches on a nail. He thought of the judge they had watched through the observation window, how she had a term, a robe, a fixed authority that did not rise or fall with the mood of the room. And he thought of Sirine's parliament, where power was held on something more like a lease. Two logics, sitting side by side on a courthouse bench, and neither of them wrong in a way he could name.

"So which is better?" he asked.

"Mine," said Bronson and Sirine at the same moment, and then they laughed, and Edouard did not, because a clerk in a gray cardigan had come to the doorway holding a clipboard and said his name.

The hallway contracted. He stood and his knees reported the hour they had spent folded. Room 4C was smaller than he expected, four rows of seats and a flaking radiator, and the case was nothing like the version he had rehearsed all week. It was about a fence, and a survey, and a tree that two neighbors each believed they owned. He was asked four questions. Had he seen the fence being replaced. On what date. From which window. Was he certain. His answers came out flat and exact, and he was aware, as he spoke, that certainty was not something he owed these people as a courtesy but something he had to give or withhold honestly, and that withholding it, saying I think so instead of yes, cost him something and bought something too.

When he came out, Bronson was standing, and Sirine had her chin in her hand, and she looked at him with an incisive squint he had never received from her before, as if he had become a slightly different person in the last nine minutes.

"Well?" Bronson said.

"Nothing happened. I said what I saw. There was a tree." He sat back down between them, and the bench felt different now, warmer, his. "It's not like your president thing. The judge can't just be removed because someone in that room disagrees with her. But she's not elected either. She's somewhere in between."

Sirine turned a seed over in her fingers without eating it. "So you're saying neither of us is right."

"I'm saying I don't know yet. Your way, the leader answers every day. His way, the leader answers on one day, and then you wait. I don't know which one I'd choose if I had to choose."

"You'd choose ours," Bronson said.

"He'd choose ours," Sirine said.

A door opened down the hall and the clerk with the gray cardigan leaned out, looked both ways, and said, "The tree man. They want you back for one more question."

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: The European Union's AI Act, which entered into force on August 1, 2024, bans some uses of AI outright, including social scoring of people.
story:
Emma set her phone face down beside her plate the way she always did, and the way her mother always pretended not to notice. Across the table sat Mr. O'Brien, the retired teacher from next door, who came Thursdays and ate their overcooked chicken as though it were a favor he was doing them. Emmitt had been invited because his parents were at his sister's recital, and he was already three bites into his potatoes when he said it.

"Did you see what they're doing at Harmon?" he said. "That school in Ohio. They run everything through software. How long you're online, what you post, who you talk to, all of it goes into a number. Kids get ranked. Top of the list gets privileges. Bottom of the list gets called in."

Emma's mother paused with the serving spoon in the air. Her father said nothing, which for him was a kind of speech.

"Like a credit score," Emmitt went on, "but for being a good student. They call it early intervention." His tone was insouciant, but he kept glancing at Emma as he said it, and she understood why. Her father worked in data analytics. Her family's whole income rested on the belief that numbers about people could be sorted into something useful.

"Sounds efficient," her father said at last.

"Sounds like being graded on existing," Emma said. She hadn't meant to say it so sharply. Mr. O'Brien looked up from his plate, and she felt the attention of the table shift to her like weather changing.

"Everything's graded," her father said. "Colleges grade you. Employers grade you. At least this is transparent."

"Transparent to whom?" She thought of the app her own school had installed on the laptops last fall, the one that logged idle time and flagged keywords. Nobody had ever explained the flagging. Emmitt had gotten called down in March, and the counselor would only say the system had "identified a concern," and Emmitt had sat there, red to the ears, insisting it was a poem he'd written. That was the part nobody at this table knew, she realized. Emmitt had never told her parents, and she had never told hers, and here he was talking about a school in Ohio instead.

Mr. O'Brien cut his chicken into smaller and smaller pieces. "In my day," he said, "the worst surveillance we had was a nun with good hearing."

"So would it even be legal?" Emma asked him. "Here, I mean. Or anywhere."

Mr. O'Brien said he didn't know, he was a Latin teacher, not a lawyer, but she should look it up rather than take an old man's word. It was the kind of thing he always said, and usually it annoyed her, but tonight she picked up the phone she'd put face down and typed with one thumb under the table. The room went on around her, her father describing some system that scored loan applicants, Emmitt arguing that any ranking at least told you where you stood. She half listened. The software, she thought, was a genus, and Ohio and her father's loan office were both species of it, and she was tired of people acting as though the species were unrelated.

The page loaded. She read it twice.

"There's a law," she said, and the table went quiet again. "The European Union's AI Act. It entered into force on August 1, 2024." The date felt strange in her mouth, official, like reading aloud in class. "It bans some uses of AI outright. Including social scoring of people."

"Meaning what?" her mother asked.

"Meaning ranking them like that. Ohio's whole system. Illegal in Europe, flat out. Not regulated. Banned."

Her father put down his fork. "Europe bans things. Europe also decided cucumbers couldn't be too curved. And they may be wrong. There may be uses of scoring that are fair."

"That's actually the interesting part," Emma said, surprising herself, because she had expected to come out swinging and instead she heard both sides arriving in her mouth at once. "Some uses, sure. If the data's clean, if everyone can see the rules, maybe a number is fairer than a teacher who just doesn't like you. Mr. O'Brien's nun with good hearing had bias too. She just didn't print it out." She looked at Emmitt when she said it, and he looked back, and she saw him decide something.

"March," he said, to her parents, to the table, to no one in particular. "I got flagged in March. They wouldn't tell me why. It was a poem."

Her father's face did something complicated that adumbrated a longer argument, a reconsideration, a pivot she could not yet read. He reached over and turned his own phone face down beside his plate, and the screen, before it went dark, showed a dashboard full of little colored dots.

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: In Darley and Latané's 1968 experiment, about 85 percent of people who thought they alone heard someone having a seizure helped, but only about 31 percent did when they thought four others heard it.
story:
Jackson was late to third period because he had stopped at the vending machines, and Mr. Ortiz did not let him pretend otherwise. "Sit," Mr. Ortiz said, tapping the sign-up sheet, and Jackson dropped into the desk beside Mackenna while Mariam stood at the front unwinding a poster she had made from butcher paper. The poster showed two circles, one much fuller than the other, and above them she had written a date in marker: 1968.

"Darley and Latané," Mariam began, her voice steadier than it had been during her last presentation. "They had people talk over intercoms, and one voice, a recording, started saying he was having a seizure. When the participants thought they were the only ones hearing it, about 85 percent went for help." She tapped the fuller circle. "When they thought four other people were listening too, only about 31 percent did." She let the number sit a moment. "Same seizure. Same person. The only thing that changed was how many people they thought were also responsible."

"That's depressing," Mackenna said.

"That's data," Mariam said.

Jackson raised his hand even though Mr. Ortiz had told him twice this semester to stop doing that, just to talk. "So they just didn't care. People are lazy."

Mariam looked at him the way she looked at a wrong answer she had expected. "The 85 percent cared. Same kind of people."

He wanted to argue. He had, in fact, already half written his rebuttal in his notebook, something about diffusion being an excuse for cowards, and he had planned to call anyone who accepted it an apologist for bad behavior. But her two circles kept floating back up when he tried to sharpen the sentence. Mr. Ortiz moved on to trade-offs, how every choice to act is a choice not to do something else, how a system can produce a bad outcome even when no single person in it is bad, and Jackson wrote nothing for the rest of the period except a small question mark.

At lunch the cafeteria had its usual diurnal roar, trays and chairs and the fryer hissing behind the counter, sunlight slanting through the high windows onto the linoleum. Jackson was unwrapping a sandwich when the boy two tables over, a sophomore he knew only as a face from the bus, made a short choked sound and slid off the bench. His head struck the floor with a knock that cut through everything.

The room did not go silent; it went strange. Conversation thinned and warped around a hole. People stood halfway up and stayed there, trays still in their hands, faces turning left and right, looking at each other, looking toward the staff door, looking everywhere except down. A girl held her phone in front of her mouth like a walkie-talkie, saying something into it, not moving. Mackenna, beside Jackson, had gone rigid, her fingers tight on the table edge, and she said, "Should somebody," and stopped, because the sentence needed an object and there were four hundred of them.

Jackson was already up. He remembered, with a clarity that felt almost physical, being eleven at the lake, his uncle shouting for someone to grab the rope, and how everyone on the dock had waited a full breath before his cousin took it, and how his uncle had said afterward that nobody was bad, there were just too many of them. He had always understood that as an excuse. Now, crossing the linoleum in five long strides, he understood it as a description.

He knelt. The boy's eyes were open and unfocused, his jaw working, and Jackson remembered the unit from health class last year and did not try to hold him still or put anything in his mouth. He turned the boy's head gently to the side, cleared the lunch tray away with his forearm, and said, "Hey. I'm Jackson. You're okay." Behind him he heard Mackenna finally yelling for the coach, her voice cracking upward, and the room came back to life in a disorderly wave, chairs scraping, someone running.

The boy's shaking slowed and stopped. He blinked at the ceiling, at Jackson's face, at the small crowd that had no shape anymore because it was dissolving into useful motions. Mariam crouched down on the boy's other side with her water bottle and her jacket folded under his head before Jackson could think to do either.

"You froze," Jackson said to Mackenna later, in the doorway, when the paramedics had come and gone and the lunch period had been declared over.

"I know."

"Me too. For like four seconds." He had counted them, in his head, without meaning to. "It's not that nobody cares. It's that everybody thinks somebody else already does."

"Is that supposed to make me feel better?"

"No," Jackson said. "It's just what happened." He looked down the emptying hallway toward the nurse's office, where the door was just closing. "I don't know if I'd have moved faster if it had been just me and him."

"You moved," Mariam said, and handed him his sandwich, which she had carried out of the cafeteria in her free hand the whole way.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Countering is when one actor shifts position to balance the stage after another actor crosses, keeping both visible to the audience.
story:
The gym smelled of floor wax and old popcorn, and Michael had taped a rectangle of the basketball key into a stage with blue painter's tape because the real stage was still holding the winter choir risers. He set his folding chair at the free-throw line, which he had decided was the audience, and he waited for Jaden and Kaylin with the script rolled in his fist like a baton. He was not a theatre person. He had signed the interest sheet in October mostly to be near people who talked about things other than stats, and then Ms. Wijaya had read his name aloud in the empty auditorium and said, "Fine, you direct the one-act," in the flat voice of someone assigning detention, and he had not known how to say no to an adult who was already walking away.

His father, when Michael mentioned it at dinner, had asked whether directing was a real thing a person could do, or whether it was more like standing around. Michael had wanted to impugn the question, to point out that somebody had to decide where everyone stood and when they spoke, but the truth was he did not yet know the answer himself, so he passed the rice and said it counted as a credit.

Kaylin arrived first, in the sneakers she wore for everything, and Jaden came in still carrying his calculus homework like a passport. The one-act was eleven minutes long, two characters arguing in a kitchen that did not exist yet, and Michael had spent the whole weekend drawing arrows in the script margins, arrows from the table to the door, arrows toward the imaginary window, until the pages looked like a play drawn by a weatherman. He had a theory of directing, assembled from half a documentary and one rehearsal he had watched through the auditorium window: the director knew things the actors did not, and told them those things until the scene obeyed.

For the first hour, this theory did not survive contact. When he said "walk to the door on that line," Jaden walked, and something happened that Michael could see but not name. Jaden crossed in front of Kaylin, and Kaylin, planted at the table, disappeared behind him, both of her and her whole argument swallowed by a boy in a hoodie, visible to no one sitting where the audience would be. "Do it again," Michael said, and it happened again, the same crossing, the same vanishing, and he felt a presentiment that this was not a fluke but a law, that the stage had rules and he was being graded on ones nobody had taught him.

"Kaylin, just, like, move when he goes," he called, which was vague, and she shifted half a step at random, which fixed nothing. He tried to think of whom he could ask. Ms. Wijaya was in her office two hallways away, and he imagined carrying the problem to her like a broken appliance, and he imagined her asking how the directing credit was going, and he stayed in his folding chair. He had wanted this to be something he could do on his own; the wanting was almost congenital, the same stubbornness that made him refuse speech lessons after the championship loss two years ago, standing in another gym, letting the buzzer settle into silence rather than join the huddle. He had walked out that night, and no one had stopped him, and he still did not know whether that had been dignity or quitting, only that the two had felt identical from inside.

So he experimented instead. "Jaden, cross again, slower." He watched not Jaden but the whole taped floor, the way he used to watch the whole court. When Jaden moved left, the stage tipped toward him, heavy on one side, Kaylin stranded out of balance on the other. "Kaylin, when he crosses, shift the other way a little. Just enough to open it back up." She did, a quarter step right as Jaden passed left, and suddenly both of them were visible, the stage level again, the scene holding air. "Again," Michael said, and they ran it four times, and each time Jaden crossed and Kaylin shifted, both faces staying alive to the empty bleachers where the audience would sit.

"It's called countering," Jaden said on the fifth pass, and Michael looked at him. "My mom did community theatre. She used to yell it from the back row." Michael wrote the word in the margin next to the weather arrows, and his ear went warm, because the thing he had worked out in the blue-taped key had a name the whole time, one Jaden could have offered at hour one. He did not say anything about that. He said, "Okay, countering on that cross, and again when you go to the window," and they ran the scene, and for about ninety seconds the kitchen that did not exist worked.

When Ms. Wijaya finally did come down the hall and lean in the gym doorway, Kaylin and Jaden were frozen mid-argument, both facing the folding chair, and Michael was standing inside the taped rectangle, one hand out like a traffic cop, silent, because he had started to believe that some of directing was knowing when not to speak. She watched for a while, arms folded. He waited for her verdict on the blue tape, on the folding chair, on the whole borrowed gym. "You found the door of the scene," she said at last, which was not English as far as he could tell, and then she was gone down the hallway. Michael looked at Jaden, then at Kaylin. "From the top," he said.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: In the United States, courts generally will not enforce a liability waiver that tries to excuse gross negligence or intentional misconduct, even if the person signed it.
story:
The waiver was one page, folded twice, and Christopher read it standing because the lobby of Apex Driving School had only two chairs and both were taken by a man watching a muted television mounted near the ceiling. The document said, in font small enough to suggest hope, that the student assumed all risk inherent in driver training, that Apex and its employees would be held harmless from any claim arising from instruction, and that signing constituted consent to these terms and conditions. Below the paragraph was a line for a parent's signature, because Christopher was seventeen.

His father had put the form on the kitchen table the night before, uncapped a pen, and then stopped with the pen hovering. "You sign this, you can't sue them if something happens," his father said. "That's how it works, right?" Christopher had said he thought so. His father had said, "Think harder," and gone to bed, leaving the form unsigned, which was how Christopher ended up in the lobby on a Saturday morning with the paper in his backpack and no signature he could use.

Zoya was there for the same nine o'clock behind-the-wheel slot, hers already signed by an aunt who, as far as Christopher could tell, signed anything put in front of her, including petitions outside grocery stores. Lilou was there because she'd failed the written test twice and was retaking it in the back room, and had come early to sit with them and complain about right-of-way questions. The three of them had known one another since middle school, in the way of people who had never chosen each other and now couldn't imagine otherwise.

"I don't actually know what I signed," Zoya said, peeling the sticker off an orange. "My aunt read maybe two words of it. One of them was probably 'the.'"

"It says they're not liable," Christopher said. "That's most of what it says. 'Liability' appears eleven times." He had counted on the bus, partly to stay awake and partly because counting felt like doing something.

Ms. Greco came out of the office at five to nine. She was the instructor, a broad woman with reading glasses pushed up into gray hair, and the first thing she did was take attendance off a clipboard, and the second thing she did was look at Christopher's unsigned form and exhale through her nose. "We can't put you in the car without it," she said. "Insurance, corporate, all of that. You need a parent."

"I know," Christopher said. "I have a question first, though. If I sign this, and something happens, is Apex responsible for anything at all? Or does the paper cover everything?"

Ms. Greco looked at him for a moment the way a chess player looks at a board where a piece has moved without permission. "The waiver covers the inherent risks," she said. "That's what it's for." She said it carefully, like someone reading from an internal script, and then the phone behind the desk rang and she went to answer it, which answered nothing.

"She dodged," Lilou said, arriving from the back room with her retake ticket and a face that said the right-of-way questions had won again. "She answered a different question than the one you asked."

Zoya already had her phone out. Her thumbs moved with the flat concentration of someone who had done research at 8:55 in the morning before, usually about teachers or ex-boyfriends. "Okay," she said after a minute. "There's a thing. Courts. In the United States, courts generally won't enforce a waiver that tries to excuse gross negligence."

"Gross negligence," Lilou repeated, in the tone of someone testing whether the words would hold weight.

"That's what it says," Zoya said. "Or intentional misconduct. Even if the person signed it. So the paper gets them out of ordinary stuff, the risks of driving itself, but not out of that." She turned the phone around so Christopher could see the screen, as if the serif font were a second witness.

Christopher took the phone and read the rest of it himself, slowly, because he had learned the hard way that Zoya summarized the way rivers summarized, keeping only the largest stones. The text said what she'd said. It did not say what counted as gross negligence versus ordinary negligence, and it did not say who decided, and he could feel the whole thing sitting there like a word problem with the final line torn off. But his father's question had been "can you sue them," and the answer was apparently "yes, for some things, no matter what the form says," and that was not nothing. That was, in fact, the difference between a form that meant what it said and a form that meant what it could get away with.

Ms. Greco came back, still holding the phone receiver against her hip. "Nine o'clock was five minutes ago," she said. "Signature or no car."

"I'll get my dad to sign tonight," Christopher said. "I'm going to tell him what the form can't actually do." He folded the waiver along its original creases and put it back in his backpack, next to a calculator he hadn't used since June. Zoya followed Ms. Greco out toward the lot, peeling her orange in one unbroken spiral, and through the window Christopher watched the little white sedan with the rooftop sign pull away from the curb, Zoya in the passenger seat adjusting the mirror like she owned it.

activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: A pocket veto happens when Congress adjourns during the president's ten-day window and the president does not sign the bill, so it does not become law.
story:
The agenda lay folded in Maika's lap, and at the top of it, item four, was the thing her whole class had been arguing about for a week: Ordinance 22-C, the skate park her brother had petitioned for and then lost somewhere in the machinery of the city. She had come to the council chamber because the council chamber was where lost things went, apparently, and she wanted to watch one either come back or disappear for good.

Alisha had come with her, mostly for the donuts the student council table was offering, and Pierce had come because Ms. Banerjee had offered extra credit and Pierce never turned down extra credit. They sat in the back row of folding chairs, under the hum of fluorescent lights that gave everything a gray film. The chamber smelled of burnt coffee and floor wax. A clock above the dais ticked in a register slightly too loud for the room.

"Here's what I still don't get," Pierce whispered, leaning across Alisha. "In class. The president never said no to that bill. It just died. Ten days went by and nobody signed anything." He flipped his notebook to a page where he'd written "???" in the margin three times, like a man knocking on a door. "How can a law die of nothing?"

"Maybe it starved," Alisha said. "Like a plant you forget to water."

Maika didn't answer right away. She was watching the clerk carry a stack of paper to the dais, and she noticed that the stack was the ordinance in three versions: the original draft, the amended draft from the parks committee, and a final clean copy. Somewhere between the first and the last, someone had changed the word "shall" to "may," and she wondered whether a whole skate park could live or die in the gap between those two words.

The meeting began with the pledge and a rubber-gavel crack that made Alisha jump. Then the council worked down the agenda with a slowness that Maika at first took for laziness and then, watching more carefully, for something closer to ceremony. Each item was introduced by its number, read aloud in part, discussed. When a man in a yellow jacket stood up during public comment and called the proposed fee structure "a rip-off dressed as a favor," the council member chairing the meeting asked him politely to address the substance, and Maika thought, so that's what a dysphemism gets you here: a correction, not an argument. He sat down, having propitiated no one, and the room moved on.

When item four came up, the chamber shifted. Kids in the front rows stopped slouching. A woman from the parks department explained the committee's changes, how the plan had been reviewed twice, once for cost and once for noise, and how the neighbors' association had asked for a fence that the skaters called a cage. "Putative neighbors," the woman said, a little dryly, "since only two of them actually live on that street," and a ripple of laughter went around the room and softened something in it.

The debate itself took forty minutes. One council member argued that the city could not afford maintenance; another read a letter from a twelve-year-old; a third asked about liability in a tone that suggested she had already decided against the whole enterprise. Maika found she was holding two opinions at once, and neither would sit down. Money was real, and so was the fact that she could name six kids within a mile who skated in the church parking lot because there was nowhere else. She kept both in her hands, turning them like coins.

Then the vote. Four to three, and the gavel came down, and the ordinance passed on its second and final reading, and Alisha grabbed Maika's sleeve and said, "It goes to the mayor now, right? He signs it?"

"He has ten days," Pierce said, checking his notebook. "If he does nothing, it still becomes law. That's how it works. Silence means yes."

And Maika, who had been rereading the handout from Ms. Banerjee's class, the one folded into the back of her agenda, felt the two halves of the thing finally meet. "Unless they adjourn," she said slowly, almost to herself. "If Congress goes home during the president's ten-day window and he never signs it, then it doesn't become law at all. It just dies. It's called a pocket veto." She looked up. "That's the answer to your question. The bill didn't die of nothing. It died because nobody was there to receive a yes."

Pierce stared at her, then wrote it down without the question marks. "So silence can mean yes or no depending on whether anyone's still in the room," he said. "That's a terrible way to run a country."

"It's kind of a beautiful way," Alisha said. "It's like the room itself gets a vote."

Maika wasn't sure she agreed with either of them, and she said so, and Alisha shrugged and handed her the last donut, which was her way of disagreeing without any of the machinery. Outside, the November dark had come down and the chamber's windows had turned to mirrors, so that the council, voting on the next item, seemed to be floating in the street among the parked cars and the sodium light.

Ms. Banerjee found them on the steps, pulling her scarf tighter. "You stayed for the whole agenda," she said. "Nobody stays for the whole agenda."

"We wanted to see if the mayor would sign it," Maika said. "The skate park."

"He'll take his ten days, I imagine. He likes to be seen deliberating." Ms. Banerjee smiled and started down the steps, and Maika stood there a moment longer, wondering whether a signature was a real thing or just a room agreeing to believe in one, and then she ran to catch up with her friends, who were already halfway to the bus stop, arguing about donuts.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Before the Eid al-Fitr prayer, Muslims who can afford it give a set charity called zakat al-fitr for each family member, so that poor families can also celebrate Eid.
story:
The night before Eid, the cultural center smelled of cardamom and floor wax, and Jackson's mother had appointed him treasurer of a small paper bag of rice. "Count heads," she said, emptying the five-kilo sack into portion after portion on the folding table. "Your father, me, you, Auntie Ruksana, the twins. Everyone eats, everyone gives." She was explaining it to Ms. Ba, who ran the center and had offered the gym for tomorrow's prayer, and who was watching the rice pile with the polite concentration of a woman taking mental notes. Jackson, meanwhile, was being careful not to look blasé about a task he privately found repetitious, because his mother could detect indifference through walls.

"It's called zakat al-fitr," his mother said to Ms. Ba, smoothing a bag closed. "A set charity for each person in the household, before the Eid prayer, so that poor families can celebrate too." Ms. Ba nodded slowly, and Jackson, bagging rice, thought about that longer than the task required. Everyone in the house, even the twins, who were four and contributed nothing to the household except noise and missing shoes. Even him. Even people who couldn't pay for themselves were paid for by someone. It was a system that assumed you belonged somewhere whether you'd earned it or not, which was, he decided, either beautiful or embarrassing depending on whether he was the four-year-old.

He got it wrong anyway. At eleven that night, sprawled on the couch texting Teresa, he did the arithmetic out loud for an audience of one. Teresa was Muslim too, and had done the same chore at her own house, so she was the wrong person to try to bluff. "Six bags," Jackson said. "Dad, Mom, me, Auntie, two twins. Six." A pause, then her reply arrived: "your cousin Asad flew in Tuesday. he's staying with you. did you seriously forget your own cousin." Jackson stared at the ceiling. Asad had been in the house since Tuesday, eating their cereal, sleeping on an air mattress that leaked with a sound like a dying accordion, and Jackson had walked past him approximately forty times without once counting him.

"That's seven," he texted back, and then, because he was honest with Teresa in a way he rarely managed with anyone else, including himself: "I think part of me just doesn't register him. Like he's furniture that talks." Her response was immediate: "wow. denigrate your own cousin. at Eid." She sent a thumbs-down emoji, then a longer message that said, more gently, that she'd once forgotten her grandmother and had to run the rice over at dawn, and that running rice through a dark neighborhood in her grandfather's sandals had cured her permanently of forgetting anyone. Jackson put the phone on his chest and listened to the accordion air mattress sighing down the hall.

The next morning the cultural center gym filled with shoes. Rows and rows of them outside the door, lining the hallway like a migration, and inside, women on one side, men on the other, and his father's coat pocket bulging with the seven bags, which Jackson had measured at midnight with the solemnity of a pharmacist. Asad stood next to him in a wrinkled kurta, hair flat on one side, whispering that the leaked air mattress was a form of torture and that Jackson should be tried at The Hague. "I counted you," Jackson whispered back. "You're in the math." Asad looked at him with genuine suspicion, and Jackson could not blame him, because the sentence, spoken aloud, was not a compliment.

They were early, so early that a strange lassitude crept in, a kind of ennui that comes from being awake before a holiday technically starts, waiting for it like a train delayed on a platform. To fight it, Jeremy showed up. Jeremy had come on a whim, having heard there would be food afterward, and stood in the hallway holding a paper cup of tea and asking questions in the tone of a documentary host. "Why is everyone giving your dad little bags?" Jackson explained it, the set charity per family member, before the prayer, so poor families could celebrate Eid too, and Jeremy nodded with the focus of a boy memorizing a fact for later use in arguments with his own family. "That's actually a really good system," he said, which was the most sincere thing Jackson had ever heard him say, and both of them were briefly embarrassed by it.

Then Teresa appeared, ostensibly to deliver something to her mother on the women's side, actually to check on him, and she did it with exquisite subtext. "So," she said, examining the bulletin board as though it were the Louvre. "Everyone made it into the count this year? No cousins left sleeping on the porch?" Asad, three feet away, narrowed his eyes. "What cousins," he said. "Who's counting cousins." Teresa smiled at the bulletin board. Jackson, standing between them, understood that he now had a choice: he could let the joke float as a harmless abstract, or he could confess, out loud, in the hallway, that he had erased a member of his own household from his family's small arithmetic, and that the erasure had felt natural until someone made him look at it.

Outside the gym doors, Ms. Ba was taping a sign that said prayer at eight sharp, please silence phones, and Jackson could hear his father somewhere near the front, handing bags over, greeting the man from the mosque who would collect them all and carry them to families Jackson would never meet. He took a breath. "I forgot you," he told Asad. "Last night. You were in the house and I didn't count you, and I had to be told, and I've been thinking about why since about midnight." Asad blinked at him. Behind them Teresa said, softly, "Solid work," and raised her paper cup. Asad looked at Jackson a moment longer, then shrugged one shoulder. "Fine," he said. "But you're pumping up that air mattress tonight, and I want it done before I finish my tea."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Chemist Michel Eugène Chevreul published his law of simultaneous contrast in 1839, describing how a color appears to shift toward the complement of the color placed next to it.
story:
Ryder had agreed to paint the backdrop for the community studio's spring show because he needed the studio's open hours more than he needed the job, and Ms. Fraser, who ran the place, knew both things and offered anyway. The backdrop was a long panel of gray, meant to sit behind the students' sculptures so that nothing would compete with their colors. He had mixed the gray himself from leftovers, titrating white into black until the swatch looked like neither, and by the second afternoon he had covered most of the panel in one unbroken field.

Maeve had claimed the table nearest the window. She was painting a stone wall in watercolor, small and patient, and she kept tilting her head at it. "It's the same gray," she said, not looking up. "Same mix, same brush, same afternoon. But here it looks like it's been sitting in the sun, and here it looks like it belongs in a hospital." She turned the paper toward him. On the left, where her wall ran beside a patch of orange roof tiles, the gray was unmistakably warm, almost dusty pink. On the right, beside a blue door, the same gray went cold and flat as slate.

Ryder came over and stood where the window light wouldn't favor either side. He looked for a long time. "It's not the light," he said. "The light's the same across the paper. It's the neighbors."

Maeve frowned. "Paint doesn't have neighbors."

"Colors do, though." He wasn't sure where he'd gotten that. Somewhere in the studio's shelf of donated books, probably, the ones nobody read, the ones with cracked spines that Ms. Fraser kept because throwing out a book went against her religion. He went to the shelf and started pulling titles. Most were technique manuals, step-by-step portraits of barns. Then he found a thin one on color, French name on the cover, Chevreul, and sat on the floor with it in the window light.

Erica arrived with her skate bag over one shoulder and dropped onto the stool beside Maeve. "Are we doing homework in here now?"

"Ryder's being a detective," Maeve said.

"His gray looks different next to different colors and he doesn't know why," Erica said, flat, already unwrapping a sandwich. "Mine does that too. I don't read a book about it, I just fix it."

"You're a pragmatist," Ryder said, still reading.

"I'm hungry," Erica said. But she leaned over his shoulder anyway.

The book was old-fashioned in its language, careful and a little stiff, but the idea was plain enough that he could say it back to himself without the book: a color appears to shift toward the complement of the color placed next to it. The gray beside the orange roof had drifted toward blue, the orange's complement, which read to the eye as cool shadow; wait, he turned the sentence over again, then looked at Maeve's paper. The gray near the orange looked warm. He checked the direction twice, and it held: the gray was being pushed toward the complement of its neighbor, and the complement of the blue door was the warm direction, so the cold patch sat beside the orange, the warm beside the blue. Whichever way the sentence ran, the paper agreed with it once he matched the pairs correctly. "It's called the law of simultaneous contrast," he said. "This chemist, Chevreul, published it in 1839." He said it not like an announcement but like setting a stone down where it fit.

Maeve took the book from him and read the page herself. "So my wall isn't wrong," she said slowly. "It's just honest about where it lives." Erica, chewing, pointed at the right side of the paper with her sandwich. "Then make it wrong on purpose. Put a little of the door color in that gray, nobody checks." Maeve said that was cheating. Erica said that was painting.

Ryder went back to his panel and stood in front of it for a while before picking up the brush. His flat gray field, the one meant to be neutral behind everything, would not be neutral at all. Behind a red sculpture it would lean one way, behind a green glaze the other, and he could not predict all of it, because the sculptures weren't chosen yet. He could see two roads from where he stood: Erica's, to adjust each section once the work was placed, section by section, a pragmatist's patchwork; or Maeve's, to leave the field alone and let it answer every neighbor differently, and call that the design. Both were defensible. He genuinely did not know which he believed, and the not knowing sat in him quietly, the way the gray sat on the panel, waiting to find out what would stand beside it.

Ms. Fraser came through with her coffee and looked at the panel for a moment. "It'll be a different gray in every spot," she said, and he nodded, and she moved on without offering an opinion, which was her way of offering one.

He decided by doing what the law itself seemed to suggest: not fighting the shifts but planning for them. He sectioned the panel lightly in charcoal, one zone for each plinth where a sculpture would sit, and where he knew a piece would be orange, he let himself warm that stretch of gray a fraction, and where the piece was blue, he cooled it, so that each field would be pushed back toward the middle by its neighbor. He could not be sure it would work until the sculptures arrived, and he told Maeve so when she asked. She was less effusive than Erica would have been, but she came and stood beside him, holding her own gray wall up next to his panel, the two of them looking at one small painted door and its stubborn, shifting patch of stone.

"Leave the door blue," Ryder said. "It's better company for that wall than any fix would be."

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: A zero derivative does not guarantee a maximum or minimum: f(x) = x cubed has derivative zero at x = 0, but its graph keeps rising through that point.
story:
The library closed at six, which gave Emile ninety minutes, and he had already spent fifteen of them watching Reanna underline the same line in her notebook. The tutoring was his idea, though not his plan. Ms. Delgado had posted a notice at the circulation desk: math help offered, Tuesdays, the table by the windows, remuneration in the form of service hours, which was the school's way of saying nobody would be paid.

"Do you actually get this," Reanna said. It was not quite a question. She had a unit test on Thursday, and the coach had made it clear that her eligibility for Saturday's meet depended on it, and she had a way of making her problems feel like weather systems that other people were also going to have to survive.

Emile sat down across from her and pulled the worksheet toward him. He had passed this unit two weeks ago, barely, and had been quietly lionized for it by exactly one person, his uncle, who told everyone at dinner that Emile was "the mathematician now," a title Emile had not asked for and could not support. The truth was he had memorized the steps. Find the derivative. Set it equal to zero. Solve. Declare a maximum. He had done it eleven times on the test and gotten eleven check marks, and he had never once looked at a graph.

"The profit one," Reanna said. "You take the derivative, it's twelve minus six x, so x equals two, and the maximum is at two." She wrote it with a flourish that suggested she believed flourish was half the grade. "Done."

"That's what I did," Emile said. "On my test. That's what I did."

"So it's right."

He wanted to say yes. He had a check mark somewhere in a folder at home that said yes. But something about watching her do it, the confidence arriving before the work instead of after it, made him unwilling to hand it over like a shortcut. He turned to the blank page at the back of her notebook. "Before we say maximum, graph it. The whole thing. Just quickly, a few points."

"We don't have time for art," Reanna said, but she was already plotting, because plotting was easier than arguing and she knew it. She marked x at zero, one, two, three, then the y values, and connected them, and the curve climbed the left side of the page, hesitated at the top of the hill, and climbed again.

"Wait," she said.

Emile was already writing his own example underneath, f of x equals x cubed, because it was the simplest thing his memory offered and he wanted to see the same hesitation in isolation. He plotted it. The curve came up from the bottom of the page, flattened almost flat at the origin, and kept rising, straight through. He took the derivative in the margin, three x squared, set it to zero, got x equals zero. He tapped the graph with his pen. The derivative was zero at that point, and there was no hill there at all. Nothing stopped. It just went through.

"So the derivative being zero doesn't mean maximum," Reanna said slowly, and Emile felt the check marks in his folder at home rearranging themselves into something less impressive. It meant the graph was flat at that point, that was all he could honestly say, and flat could be the top of a hill or the middle of a climb. His eleven correct answers had been correct the way a stopped clock is correct.

"That's going to be on the test," Reanna said. "Ms. Delgado put it on the review sheet, look, question nine." She spun the sheet toward him. Question nine asked for the graph of a cubic, and beneath it, in the answer key printed upside down at the bottom, the curve rose through its flat point without pausing.

"Then what do we do," Reanna said. "If the derivative is zero and it might not be a maximum, how do you ever know?"

Emile tested the values on either side, the way he'd seen done once and half understood: numbers greater than two gave a negative derivative, numbers less than two gave a positive one, so the profit function really did turn over at two, for that one. He showed her. He could not have explained why it worked, only that it had, and he said so out loud, which surprised them both. Reanna tried it on her own function, chewing her pen, the diaphanous curtain at the window moving behind her in the ventilation like the library itself was breathing. She got it right.

"Okay," she said. "Question ten. And you're explaining it like someone who just learned it, which is actually better, no offense."

"Complete offense," Emile said, and she laughed, and they did question ten.

At five fifty, Ms. Delgado came by with her keys already in her hand, the signal that the library's patience had a derivative and it had just hit zero. On the table between them, Reanna's notebook lay open to the cubic, its curve still climbing off the edge of the page toward wherever the paper ran out.

"Same time Tuesday," Reanna said, shoving the notebook into her bag. "I'll bring my own pen. The one you let me borrow smells like grape."

She walked out through the security gates, which beeped once at her bag and once at her, and Emile sat there a moment longer, copying the cubic into his own notebook, drawing the flat point with a small circle around it, then adding, underneath, in handwriting he hoped nobody would ever lionize: check the graph first, always, from now on.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The US average adjusted cohort graduation rate for public high school students was 87 percent in the 2021-22 school year.
story:
The paper plates had diplomas printed on them, which meant that by the end of the night everyone would be eating cake off their own names. Coralie's grandmother had found them at a party store two towns over, along with a banner that said CONGRATULATIONS GRADUATE in a font usually reserved for used car dealerships. Coralie's mother had hung it over the doorway to the dining room so that everyone entering had to duck slightly, as if bowing.

"A whole table just for you," said her aunt, steering her toward the corner where the folding chairs had been set up. "Famous for one night."

Reid had arrived first, holding a card with a twenty folded inside it, and had claimed the chair nearest the food. Arvin came twenty minutes later with his tie already loosened and a story about parking three blocks away because every relative in the county apparently had a child graduating. Between them they had taken eight of the chairs, and cousins kept rotating through the remaining ones, eating and leaving, so that the table's population changed like weather.

"Look at this," Reid said somewhere between the pasta and the chicken. He had his phone out, tilted so Arvin could see. "Someone posted the freshman yearbook photo. Guess who."

The photo was of Devon Ellis, age fourteen, braces and a hoodie with the strings pulled tight so only his eyes showed. Somebody in the class group chat had posted it with a crying-laughing face, and beneath it a thread of other people had added their own freshman photos, a sedimentary accumulation of bad haircuts layering down the screen, the oldest and most embarrassing at the bottom.

"He'd have hated this," Arvin said. "He hated being photographed even then."

"He'd have commented something brutal on every single one," Coralie said. She took the phone and scrolled. Devon had left their school sometime junior year; nobody in the thread had said when, exactly, or where he'd gone, only variations on miss this guy and remember when he put the frog in Mr. Wiśniewski's filing cabinet. The frog story got eleven separate replies.

Mr. Wiśniewski himself was at the party, having lived next door since Coralie was six and having been asked by her mother, in a way that permitted no refusal, to come for dinner. He was on his third helping of potatoes and telling the frog story to Coralie's father, who had heard it twice already and laughed both times as though for the first time.

"There were four of them who started with us and didn't finish," Arvin said. He was counting on his fingers. "Devon, that girl who moved to Texas, the guy from bio, and, um, the one who was always in the weight room."

"Marcus," Reid said.

"Marcus. Right." Arvin put down his fork. "That's weird to count."

"Statistically not weird at all," Coralie said. "The US average adjusted cohort graduation rate for public high school students was 87 percent in the 2021-22 school year. We're basically a spreadsheet."

"You memorized that," Arvin said.

"I looked it up in March when I was avoiding a history essay." She reached across Reid for the bread. "Thirteen out of every hundred just don't finish. It's not a tragedy exception, it's a whole shelf of people."

Her grandmother, who had been shuffling past with a tray of stuffed peppers, stopped. "Eighty-seven," she repeated. "That seems low."

"That seems high to me," said Mr. Wiśniewski, and for a moment the whole corner of the table argued about it, her grandmother insisting it was a scandal, Mr. Wiśniewski saying he'd taught for thirty-one years and that keeping eighty-seven out of a hundred in their seats until June was, in his professional opinion, a small miracle, at which her grandmother called him a cynic and he ate another potato in a way that suggested total peace with the charge.

Coralie had been accepted early to a state university with a scholarship that covered tuition but not housing, and her parents had spent the spring speaking about the commute, an hour each way by bus, as though it were a settled and convenient arrangement. Tonight her mother kept saying "when she's at the university" in a tone that implied Coralie was already there, already gone, and Coralie kept not correcting her, partly out of kindness and partly because she had not yet decided whether to say the thing she had been not deciding for two months.

Around nine o'clock the cake came out, her name in icing on the top, and everyone sang, and her grandmother cried in the way that could turn on and off like a tap, off for the photos, on for the hug. Coralie looked over her grandmother's shoulder at the wall of cousins, at the family phenotype assembled in one room, her own narrow jaw repeated on seven different faces, and felt the strange fatigue of a day that had enervated her without containing a single difficult task. Cutting the cake, she portioned the first slice large and set it aside for later, when the house would be quieter.

Reid and Arvin found her on the porch afterward with the plate, eating it with one of the diploma forks.

"So are you commuting or dorming," Arvin said. It was not a question mark kind of question; he had a way of dropping sentences like coins.

"I told my parents I'd decide by Friday," she said. "I keep doing the thing where I make both decisions and then sit between them." She ate a forkful. "Eighty-seven percent finish. Nobody publishes the number for how many finish the thing they actually wanted."

"That's because it's terrible," Reid said. "That number is like four."

"It's not four."

"It's four," Arvin said. "Reid did the math in study hall once. Ask him about the napkin."

The porch light drew moths against the screen. Inside, her mother laughed at something, the sound coming through the door with the warmth of the kitchen behind it. Coralie set the plate on the railing and pulled out her phone, and typed, to her mother, sitting ten feet away: I want to try the dorm. We can talk about the money tomorrow. Then she locked the screen and put it face down, and picked the fork back up.

"You sent it?" Arvin said.

"I sent it."

"Then give me the corner piece," Reid said. "Decision like that, you owe me a corner piece."

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Arabic newspapers across many countries are written in Modern Standard Arabic rather than local spoken dialects, so one written form serves readers in different regions.
story:
The newspaper arrived at his grandfather's door in Casablanca every morning before Olivier was awake, and on the third day of the visit his grandfather set it beside his coffee and said, in the Arabic Olivier had grown up hearing on Sunday phone calls, "Read me something. Anything on the first page."

Olivier had promised Ms. Zhu he would keep up his Arabic over the summer. She had assigned him a short article a week from an online paper, a summary spoken aloud and recorded, so that by the time he reached her intermediate class in the autumn he would not have slid back to nothing. He had managed two articles in June, both laborious, both read in his bedroom in Ohio with a dictionary open on his knee. Here, with his grandfather waiting, the page looked different. He began the lead story, about a summit of ministers, and within two sentences he felt the ground shift beneath him. Words he was certain he knew arrived wearing strange clothing. He pronounced "this" the way he had always said it at home, and his grandfather winced, gently, the way he winced when Olivier put too much sugar in his tea.

"That's not how we say it," his grandfather said. "But keep going. You're reading it right."

Olivier stopped, finger on the column. "How can I be reading it right and saying it wrong?"

His grandfather tapped the paper's masthead. "This is written in fusha. Classical, standard. The newspaper language. We speak Moroccan at home, on the street. Different rivers, same water."

He let that sit while his grandfather drank his coffee. Later that morning, walking to the market to buy mint and bread, Olivier texted Jayde, who had taken Arabic at the same school and would understand: "Turns out the newspaper isn't in the Arabic my jidi speaks. One written form for everyone, everywhere apparently, but nobody talks like that at home." Jayde replied with a screenshot from Antonio, who was in Cairo with his own family and had photographed a kiosk with a dozen different papers, all of them, Antonio claimed, in that same shared written Arabic, even though Antonio's grandmother in Alexandria said things Jaday's grandmother in Rabat would never say. Two countries, one page, Olivier thought, and felt something beguile him in the old sense, the way a puzzle beguiles before it teaches.

He went back to the article that afternoon. His grandfather had left it folded to the summit story, and beside it a pen. He read the first paragraph again, slowly, letting the formal shapes stand as themselves rather than forcing them into the rhythms of the kitchen. It was, he decided, a little like the difference between how his teachers talked at school and how Jayde and Antonio talked in the parking lot, except that in Arabic the split was codified, deliberate, a written language spanning many countries while the spoken ones stayed local. He tried the summary aloud anyway, halting, mixing registers without meaning to, and his grandfather corrected him now and then but mostly listened, chin in hand, the late sun coming through the shutters in long stripes.

There was a girl who worked at the café down the street, maybe nineteen, who was studying journalism at the university. When Olivier went in for a Coke, she saw the folded paper under his arm and switched without ceremony into French, then English, then, when he attempted his summary in Arabic, back into the local dialect with an amusement that was not unkind. "Your fusha is better than mine," she said. "Mine is all school. Yours has a grandparent in it."

"Both, maybe," Olivier said. "Half school, half grandparent."

"Everyone here is half and half," she said, and turned to the machine.

He recorded himself that evening on his phone for Ms. Zhu, two minutes of summary about ministers and ports, and listened back once. It was not good. He mispronounced one word so badly it became another word, and his transitions were parsimonious to the point of vanishing, just "and then, and then." But somewhere in the middle, for one full sentence, the reading had felt less like translation and more like standing in a room. He thought about texting Jayde some grand statement about language and time, the zeitgeist of a whole region arriving daily on his grandfather's doorstep in a form no one spoke aloud, but he deleted the draft, because he was not sure he understood it yet, and pretending would be a kind of theft.

The next morning he was awake before the paper. He waited on the step with his grandfather in silence, and when the boy on the bicycle came down the lane, Olivier stood up and took it himself.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: The area under the curve y equals x squared, from x equals 0 to x equals 1, is exactly one third.
story:
The library closed at six, and the calculus test was at nine the next morning, which gave Maxime roughly eleven hours, minus sleep, minus dinner, minus the panic that kept swallowing time like a drain. He spread his notes across the table by the window: rectangles, sums, the notation he had copied from the board without understanding, all sigmas and narrow brackets. Somewhere in there was the idea of an integral, which the textbook said found the area under a curve, and which his mind kept sliding off the way a key slides past a lock.

Antonia dropped into the chair opposite him with a muffin and no apology. "You look like the graph of a function nobody wants to integrate," she said. He told her that was not even a sentence, and she said it didn't have to be, she was here for moral support and the last blueberry. He let her have half.

He had seen this before, he realized, turning his pencil over and over. Last spring, at his grandfather's house, he had sat at the kitchen table with a sheet of graph paper while his grandfather cooked, and they had tried to estimate the area under the curve y equals x squared, between zero and one, by counting little squares. His grandfather had drawn the parabola freehand, a smooth rising hook, and Maxime had shaded everything beneath it and counted the small boxes, half-boxes, slivers. He remembered the total landing near a third of the whole square, and he remembered his grandfather saying, "Close. It is exactly one third." Exactly. Not approximately, not close enough. A curving, untidy thing pinned down by a clean number.

That was the part he couldn't reconcile. In physics the numbers were always approximate, measurements with error bars, answers that wobbled depending on how carefully you read the ruler. But his grandfather had said exactly, the way you'd say a chess rule or the number of days in June. Maxime had assumed, at the time, that the old man was rounding in his favor.

He pulled a fresh sheet and drew the square from zero to one, then the parabola, then divided the base into strips, the way the textbook had. The strips made rectangles that were sometimes too tall, sometimes too short, and when he added them he got close to a third but never a third. Antonia leaned over his shoulder. "You're counting squares again," she said. "Like a little kid."

"Like a scientist," he said. "I'm approximating."

"Ms. Ross would say you're suffering."

Ms. Ross did say something like that, later, when she passed their table on her way to shelve returns and paused, arms full of books, at the sight of his increasingly frantic strip-counting. She looked at his page for a long moment, then at the clock, then at him. "You've done it the honest way," she said. "You've bounded it." She tapped the margin where he'd written both his undercount and his overcount. "The notation in chapter six is just a way of writing what happens when those bounds get squeezed together. Nobody's asking you to take it on faith. You've already done the hard part with a pencil." Then she moved on, because the library rules said she couldn't coach them during study hall, and because the clock said five thirty and the desk said she still had forty holds to sort.

Maxime sat with that. He had been treating the integral as a piece of chicanery, a trick the textbook performed with symbols to produce an answer his squares could only approach, and he had resented it, the same way he resented when his father transliterated his grandfather's stories into English and lost the rhythm of the original. But that wasn't quite what was happening here. The strip-counting and the notation were not rivals. The counting was the argument, slow and muddy, walking the riverbank step by step; the integral was the map drawn afterward, the riparian line traced in one stroke, summarizing every step without replacing them. Maybe. He wrote one third beside his drawing of y equals x squared, between zero and one, and then, underneath, the integral with its bounds, and let the two sit next to each other on the page like the same person's two names.

He still wasn't sure he believed the exactly part. He could see that the strips could be made thinner forever, and he could see that this squeezed his two estimates toward each other, but the forever was the part his mind wouldn't hold still for, and he was honest enough with himself to write a question mark in the margin rather than pretend. The clock read 5:52. Antonia closed her muffin wrapper and stood. "Eight minutes," she said. "Decide what you're taking home."

He slid the sheet with the parabola into his binder, question mark and all, and left the strips behind on the table. "The one with the squares," he said.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In Arthur Aron's 1997 study, pairs of strangers took turns asking each other 36 questions that grew gradually more personal, and they ended up feeling closer than pairs making small talk.
story:
Hudson arrived at the mall twenty minutes early, which he understood immediately to be a tactical error, because it gave him twenty minutes to rehearse disasters. He walked past the fountain twice, straightened the collar of the one shirt his mother had not commented on, and checked his phone where Jalen's last message still sat there: just be yourself, but like, the version of yourself that talks. Cristiano had offered different advice the day before, something about listening more than he spoke, and the two suggestions had been circling each other in his head ever since, refusing to merge into anything usable.

She was already at the coffee shop table when he came back through, a little early herself, stirring a drink she hadn't really started. They had met in the line at this same place eleven days ago, when the mall was so crowded that her elbow had found his ribs and his apology had somehow turned into a conversation about the bad music playing overhead. That conversation had gone well. He had proof of nothing since.

The first fifteen minutes were fine. Then the latte foam situation on her cup apparently required her full attention, and he asked about her school, and she asked about his, and both answers arrived and departed like trains neither of them had planned to catch. He felt the silence coming the way you feel weather, something that had been gathering elsewhere and now arrived without asking. He thought about Jalen's talking version of himself, tried it, heard himself describe his locker combination, and abandoned the effort mid-sentence, which she politely pretended not to notice.

"There's this thing," he said finally, and then stopped, because starting with there's this thing sounded like a magic trick. "Sorry. Okay. My friend Jalen told me about it. This psychologist, Arthur Aron, in 1997, he had pairs of strangers take turns asking each other thirty-six questions, and the questions got gradually more personal, like step by step. And afterward the pairs who did that felt closer than the pairs who just made small talk." He turned his cup a quarter rotation on the table. "We're kind of out of small talk. Which might be a bad sign, or might just mean the small talk bucket is empty. So. Do you want to try it? Not all thirty-six. We don't have that kind of time before the mall closes."

She looked at him for a second with an expression he couldn't read, and he prepared himself for the version of this where she said that was the strangest thing anyone had ever suggested to her at a coffee shop. Instead she set down her spoon. "Thirty-six questions that get more personal," she said. "And it beat small talk. That's the whole study?" "That's the whole study." "Fine," she said. "But I go first."

Her first question was careful, the kind of thing you could ask a stranger on a bus, and he answered it honestly anyway, and then his was one notch harder, and hers was harder than that, and the mechanism of it, or whatever it was, carried them upward without anyone having to push. She was afraid of deep water but had never told anyone except her sister. He had cried at his grandfather's funeral and then lied to his aunt about the wind. Somewhere around the question of what they would each do with a free year, the mall's speakers switched to something slow and quiescent over the fountain noise, and neither of them reached for the sugar this time.

What he noticed, sitting there, was that the two pieces of advice had not been opposites at all, only halves. Talking only worked if the talking was true; listening only worked if you gave the other person something worth hearing. The study, he guessed, had built both into its staircase of questions, and Jalen and Cristiano had each handed him one stair. Whether the method was what was doing this, or whether she was just easier to be with than he had feared, he honestly could not tell from the inside, and he decided that not knowing was survivable.

When the overhead lights dimmed for closing, she checked the time on her phone and made a small sound of protest. "We never got to thirty-six," she said. "We got to maybe twelve." "We could continue the study," Hudson said, and heard how formal it came out, and kept going anyway. "Pending further trials. Next Saturday." She smiled at her cup, then at him. "That's not how studies work. You'd need a control group." "We'll find you a small talk table," he said. "For comparison."
