She stood, gathered her jacket, and paused with one hand on the back of her chair. "Last one," she said. "Question thirteen. Was this a date?" Hudson held the door for her into the parking lot, where the sodium lamps were coming on one by one along the rows. "I was hoping you'd ask that one."

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: In 1896, Swedish scientist Svante Arrhenius made the first calculation of how much Earth would warm if the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere doubled.
story:
Coralie spread the printout on the picnic table in her backyard and weighted the corners with two terra-cotta pots and a fist-sized rock. The graph ran from 1900 to the present, one thin line climbing in small sawtooth steps, dipping each year like a held breath, then rising again. She had promised Ms. Tan a five-minute explanation for tomorrow's class, and so far she could say only that the line went up.

Jimmy arrived first, carrying his bike helmet and half a bag of chips. He sat on the table's edge and looked at the paper upside down. "That's it? That's what everyone's upset about, one squiggle."

"That squiggle is carbon dioxide in the atmosphere," Coralie said. "Parts per million. Every year, averaged over the whole planet."

"So explain why it matters. That's the part I don't get. Why does more of this gas make it hotter?"

Elissa came through the gate before Coralie could answer, and she had her phone out already, which was how she entered most conversations. She dropped onto the bench, read the graph right side up, and said nothing for a moment, which for Elissa was remarkable.

Coralie tried the analogy she'd built the night before, the one with the blanket. Shortwave sunlight comes through the atmosphere and warms the ground, she said, and the ground radiates heat back outward as infrared, but some gases absorb that outgoing heat and re-emit it, part of it downward, so the surface ends up warmer than it would be with nothing overhead. She moved her hands through it, palm down for sunlight, palm up for the trapped warmth, and Jimmy nodded slowly, the way he nodded when he was deciding whether to argue.

"Okay, but people figured this out with satellites, right?" he said. "Supercomputers. It's all modern."

Elissa's thumbs were already moving. "Wait, wait. At the planetarium thing last month somebody asked exactly that, whether the predictions only started with computers, and the guy said no. I remember because I looked it up on the bus." She scrolled, frowned, scrolled again. "Here. In 1896, a Swedish scientist named Svante Arrhenius made the first calculation of how much Earth would warm if the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere doubled."

Jimmy stopped chewing. "Eighteen ninety-six. That's before cars."

"Before cars," Coralie said. She took the phone, read the sentence twice, and something rearranged itself behind her eyes. She had been thinking of the graph as a modern alarm, something that began with the instruments that measured it, and now the idea had a lineage that ran back past the first data point on her page, to a man with pencil and paper doing arithmetic on an atmosphere nobody had yet perturbed. The line on the table was not the beginning of anything. It was the middle.

"So he just did it with math," Jimmy said. "No satellites, no nothing."

"He didn't need to watch it happen to work out what would happen." Coralie set the phone down next to the rock. "That's actually better for my presentation. I was going to say, look at this scary graph. Instead I can say, we knew what doubling would do before the graph even started." She paused. "I should be careful, though. I don't know everything he got right or wrong. I only know he did the first calculation of the doubling."

"You're allowed to say what you don't know?" Jimmy said. "In a presentation?"

"She means she's not going to pretend," Elissa said. "Which, honestly, would make me trust her more."

They worked through the afternoon. Coralie practiced the blanket explanation twice, and the second time she interposed the graph itself, holding it up between her down-going and up-going hands, so the paper became the atmosphere and the table became the Earth, and Jimmy said that finally made sense to him. Elissa drilled her on the axis labels. Near five o'clock Coralie's little brother came out and started digging at the corner of the yard where the soil was loose and friable, easy to crumble between his fingers, and the sound of it made her think of something.

"I changed my mind about something," she said. "I kept saying people don't get it because the science is complicated. But it's not, really. A blanket, a graph, a guy in 1896. Complicated is not the problem."

Elissa looked up. "Then what is?"

"I don't know yet. That's the part I'm still figuring out." Coralie gathered the pots and the rock off the printout, folded the graph along the sawtooth line, and put it in her back pocket. Jimmy held the gate open for her brother, who came in with dirt to his elbows and both fists full of nothing.

"You're going to be good tomorrow," Jimmy said.

"Ask me again after fifth period," Coralie said, and she went inside to wash up.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: The derivative of a constant is zero, so adding 7 to a function shifts its graph up but leaves its derivative unchanged.
story:
Ms. Paquette set the problem on the whiteboard before anyone had taken their jackets off: a polynomial whose graph rose, flattened, and fell away again, and beneath it, the instruction to find where the curve reached its highest point. "Differentiation," she said, "is how you ask a function where it peaks." Then she sat at her desk and graded quizzes, because math club was not a class, and she had decided long ago that its members learned more when she stayed out of the way.

Addison had come late to this. She had spent the whole year watching Ryker and Ashlynn sign up for competitions while she stayed in the library, telling herself she preferred epidemiology, the study of how diseases spread through populations, which she had chosen as the topic of her biology term paper. But the paper had been finished since Sunday, and Tuesday afternoons had begun to feel like a room with nothing in it. So here she was, third row, with a borrowed textbook open to a chapter on derivatives that she had read twice on the bus.

Ryker worked fast, hunched over his page, pencil clicking against the desk whenever he stopped to think. Ashlynn worked slowly and asked questions of nobody in particular. Addison worked somewhere in between, and she had noticed, while reading, that the rules were less like rules than like a small set of honest observations. You brought the exponent down, you subtracted one, and each term took care of itself. It reminded her of the term paper: small pieces of behavior that you could count, out of which a whole population's rise and fall became visible.

"Three x squared minus twelve x," Ryker announced, leaning back. "That's the derivative."

"Three x squared minus twelve x," Ashlynn read off her own page, then looked up, then looked at his. "Wait. Mine's the same. That means one of us copied."

"I was on the other side of the room."

"Then one of us is wrong." Ashlynn turned her sheet around and held it beside his. Addison, sitting close enough to see both, noticed something before either of them did. The functions at the top of their pages were different. Ryker had copied the expression from the board and dropped a seven somewhere in the middle of his transcription; Ashlynn had kept it. Yet below the different functions, their derivative lines matched exactly, term for term, all the way down.

"Yours is missing the plus seven," Ashlynn said. "So your derivative should be wrong. But it's the same as mine."

"Then yours is wrong too," Ryker said, though he said it without conviction, because sameness was sameness, and both of them knew enough to distrust a coincidence that clean.

Addison pulled her page toward herself and, without announcing it, added seven to her own function and redid the work beneath. The derivative came out identical to her first attempt. She crossed nothing out. She sat very still with the two columns of matching numbers in front of her, and it was in that stillness that the thing assembled itself, not as a rule she had been told but as something she had seen happen. Adding seven to a function lifts its graph straight up, and the steepness at every point stays what it was. A constant sits there like a building's floor number; the slope of the stairs doesn't care which floor you started from. She thought of a moment from eighth grade, standing in a stairwell during a fire drill, her math teacher saying that a horizontal line was the flattest thing there was, and Addison had not understood then what flatness had to do with anything. She understood now that flat meant zero, and that zero meant no change, and that a number sitting by itself contributed nothing to the slope. She did not know yet whether she could say this out loud.

"It's the seven," she said. Both of them looked at her. "The derivative of a constant is zero. So adding seven shifts the whole graph up but leaves the derivative the same." Ryker frowned at his page. Ashlynn checked Addison's two columns, then her own, then said, quietly, as though conceding a point in a game that had stopped being a game, "So neither of us is wrong."

The problem wanted a maximum, though, and that was still ahead of them. Addison set the derivative equal to zero and solved it in three lines, then used the result to name the point where the curve leveled off, higher than everything around it. She checked it against the shape Ms. Paquette had drawn, and it landed where the drawing peaked. Under the desk, where neither of the others could see, she wrote the plus seven back into her original function, then crossed it out, then wrote it again, because she could not yet decide whether the version with the constant and the version without were two different problems or one problem wearing two outfits.

Ms. Paquette rose from her desk, collected nothing, and paused at the whiteboard on her way to the window. She looked at the three heads bent together over Addison's page, at Ryker's pencil clicking again, at Ashlynn copying the derivative line into her notes with the care of someone transcribing something fragile. She erased nothing and said nothing. Outside, a lawn mower started up somewhere down the block, and the chalk dust drifting past the window caught the late light and hung there, thin and friable, above the graph of a curve that had already begun, in Addison's margins, to climb again.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Circumlocution, describing a word you cannot remember instead of stopping, is a recognized communication strategy that keeps a second-language speaker talking.
story:
The restaurant had emptied after the dinner rush, and Brooklyn had claimed the corner booth as if it were a stage. Harman sat across from her with a stopwatch on his phone, Finnley beside him with a napkin covered in Spanish vocabulary she was supposed to quiz Brooklyn on between rounds. Ms. Whitaker, their Spanish teacher, had agreed to meet them here on the condition that they order something, and she was working through a bowl of soup at the counter, listening without looking over, which was somehow worse.

"On Monday you get the topic, and Tuesday you speak for five minutes," Harman said. "Five minutes, no English, on whether the city should lower the voting age to sixteen." He tapped the phone. "Ready?"

Brooklyn had wanted this slot on the debate team since fall, when she had watched a senior argue in Spanish at the regional exhibition and understood, for the first time, maybe ten percent of what was said. That had not felt like failure. It had felt like a door standing ajar. Since then she had done flashcards on the bus and conjugations in the margins of her chemistry notes, and her syntax had grown sturdier, though her accent still collapsed whenever she got nervous, the vowels flattening into something midwestern and apologetic.

"Está bien," she said. "Empieza."

Harman began the timer and read the topic in clumsy but serviceable Spanish, then switched to English for the rules. She was to argue in favor. Brooklyn opened her mouth, and the word she needed, the word she had known cold two hours ago, simply was not there.

She wanted to say that sixteen-year-olds paid taxes on their paychecks. The word for tax, impuesto, had evaporated. Panic began to metastasize through the whole sentence, taking first the noun, then the verb she had planned to hang it on, then her confidence in every word she still had. She watched Finnley's face start to crinkle with sympathy, and sympathy, in that moment, felt lethal.

"Dinero que las personas dan al gobierno," she heard herself say instead, "cada año, de su trabajo, para escuelas y calles." Money that people give the government, every year, from their work, for schools and streets. She kept going. Her rhythm stuttered, her accent wobbled, but the sentence held, and she built the next one on top of it, and the next. At some point Harman stopped checking his phone and just watched her. When she finished, forty seconds short of five minutes, she realized she had not stopped once.

From the counter, Ms. Whitaker set down her spoon. "What you just did has a name," she said. "Circumlocution. Describing a word you can't remember instead of stopping. It's a recognized strategy, and you found it on your own." Finnley wrote it on the napkin and held it up like a prize.

Brooklyn turned the word over in her mind while the waiter refilled their water, unasked, which felt like a small kindness from the universe. She had always believed that fluency meant never stumbling, and tonight had shown her something more complicated: that the stumbling could be shaped, that talking around a missing word was not the same as failing. Against the voting age itself, though, she was suddenly less sure. Sixteen-year-olds paid taxes, yes, but she also knew Harman's brother, seventeen, who couldn't be trusted with a blender. She could argue the position and hold the doubt at the same time, she supposed, the way she could speak the language and lose pieces of it and still be understood.

"One more round," she said, pushing her glass aside and squaring her shoulders against the vinyl of the booth. "This time you give me the other side, and you make it bellicose. Quiero pelear."

Finnley grinned and flipped the napkin over to its blank side. "Contra el voto a los dieciseis," she said, clicking the pen. "Empieza cuando estés lista."

activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
knowledge_domain: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
fact: Opportunity cost counts only the single next-best alternative given up, not all the alternatives added together.
story:
The appointment had been Ava's own idea, which she repeated to herself in the hallway outside the guidance office, because it sounded like something a capable person would do. Ms. Sato's door was propped open with a rubber wedge, and inside there was a desk, two chairs, a poster about deadlines, and a window that looked out on the parking lot where the buses idled. Ava sat down with her phone in her lap and a page of numbers she had worked out during study hall.

"I have three shifts I can take this weekend," she said. "Saturday morning at the bakery, Saturday night at the theatre, or Sunday at the garden centre. I can only do one, because they all collide." She turned the page toward Ms. Sato. "So I made a column. If I take the bakery, I lose the theatre money and the garden centre money, plus Riley's tournament, plus the history reading, plus sleep. I added it all up and it comes to something like two hundred and eighty dollars and an entire weekend of everything else. That can't be right. Nobody would ever choose anything."

Ms. Sato did not take out a form, which Ava had half expected. She leaned back and said, "Who told you to add it all up?"

"Nobody. It just seemed like that was the honest way to do it. The full cost." Ava looked at her column again, the long chain of losses she had assembled, and felt the peculiar weight of arithmetic she didn't trust. On the far side of the parking lot, a groundskeeper was wrestling a hose that had kinked, and the water sprayed sideways in a capricious arc before he got it under control.

Riley had texted her four times that morning about the tournament. Riley's club team had made the regional bracket for the first time in three years, and Riley, who had been benched most of the fall with a torn ligament, was starting. Ava had watched Riley relearn how to run, slowly, through a winter of grey pavement and small complaints, and she knew what Sunday would mean to her. Riley had not said you have to come. Riley never said things like that. She only sent the schedule with a single question mark after it.

"The theatre shift pays the most," Ava said slowly, working it out aloud with her finger on the page. "So if I do the bakery, the thing I'm giving up isn't the theatre plus the garden centre plus everything. It's just the theatre. Because if I hadn't chosen the bakery, the best thing I would have done is the theatre. The garden centre never happens either way. You can't lose something twice." She sat back. "Why did I think I had to expropriate my whole weekend into the cost of one shift?"

Ms. Sato smiled slightly. "I don't know. Why did you?"

"Because it felt more serious. Like if I only counted one loss, I was letting myself off." Ava crossed out the column. In her economics class they had covered the word itself, and she said it now, testing it: "Opportunity cost. I remember Johan saying it in class when everyone else was half asleep. He was the one who argued with the textbook." Johan, who planned to study labour history, who had called their town a small plutocracy run by the three families who owned the car dealership and the plaza and the gym, and who meant it as a joke and also did not.

"Then there's the tournament," Ms. Sato said.

"The tournament doesn't pay anything." Ava said it, and then heard it, and pressed her palm flat on the desk. "Except the theatre is what I'd give up if I went to the tournament. That's the real comparison. Theatre money against Riley's first start in a year." She looked out the window. The buses were pulling out in a line, one after another, each taking a route the others would never touch, and she thought about how each bus only ever followed one road.

She still didn't know. The money was for the class trip in the spring, which her mother had not offered to cover and which Ava had decided, with a private stubbornness, not to ask about. That was real. Riley on the sideline with her knee wrapped, watching, was also real. Ms. Sato handed her a hall pass without being asked and said the door was open Thursday if she wanted to talk it through again, and Ava stood, folded the page once, and put it in her pocket, the crossed-out column still legible through the fold.

In the hallway she stopped by the water fountain, took out her phone, and typed to Riley: "Tell me what time you're on the field Sunday."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Jeffrey Hall's 2018 study estimated that moving from casual friend to friend takes about 90 hours together.
story:
Thomas counted the hours on the bus to Ridgefield, because there was nothing else to count. Forty hours since the last time he and Finley sat on the tailgate of Ali's truck, and before that maybe two hundred over the summer, enough that he had stopped calculating at all. Now he did arithmetic instead of sleeping. His mother had circumscribed his first week with rules, no driving alone, home by nine, join something, as if a schedule could hold a person together.

The something turned out to be the robotics club, which met Tuesdays and Thursdays in a classroom that smelled of solder and orange peels. Thomas had not touched a circuit board since eighth grade. He signed up anyway, and the sheet on Ms. Abdi's door asked for his name in a box small enough that he wrote it carefully, like a signature on something binding.

The first Tuesday, nobody spoke to him except Ms. Abdi, who said, "You're the new one. Grab a screwdriver." He spent the hour sorting screws into a tray while three kids he would later know as Danby, Okafor, and Priya argued about gear ratios. It struck him that friendship here would be built the way the robot was, part by part, fastener by fastener, and that he had no idea how long it took.

At home he looked it up, half expecting a dead end, and found instead a study by a researcher named Jeffrey Hall. Moving from casual friend to friend took about ninety hours together. Ninety. He sat with the number a while. If the club met two hours, twice a week, that was four hours, so twenty-two weeks, nearly the whole school year. He did the division twice, then a third time, hoping the answer would shrink.

On Thursday he stayed after the official end, wiping down the workbench while Danby coiled wire and complained about the design. "You going to be one of those kids who shows up and leaves?" Danby said, not unkindly. "No," Thomas said. "I'm going to be here." He heard the incipient lie in it, because he did not yet know if he could mean it, but saying it out loud felt like turning a screw a quarter turn past hand-tight.

The trouble was that being somewhere was not the same as being with someone. He discovered this over the following weeks, watching Priya and Okafor fall into conversations that had started years ago and never really ended, references to a substitute teacher from sixth grade, a field trip where the bus broke down. Thomas existed at the edge of these, laughing at the right moments, handing over the wire strippers. He began to wonder whether the ninety hours counted only hours of actual company, or whether there was some finer unit underneath, some measure of what happened inside an hour. He wondered how anyone had measured it at all, whether they had asked people to remember, and whether memory rounded up.

In mid-October, Ali texted a photo of the truck's tailgate with Finley sitting on it alone, and Thomas typed three replies and deleted each one. The fourth said only, "Looks the same." He felt the distance as a physical fact, the way cold is a fact, and he understood something he had not before: the hours behind him with Finley and Ali were already spent, banked, and no new ones were being added, so their friendship was either finished or preserved, and he could not tell which. With Danby and Priya and Okafor the hours were incipient, barely begun, four and six and then ten, a debt of eighty more.

At the November competition, the robot's arm failed in the second round, a servo stripped under load, and Thomas was the one kneeling on the gym floor with a multitool while Priya held the flashlight and Okafor narrated the countdown. They did not win. On the bus back, dark outside, Danby passed around a bag of pretzels and said, "Worst wiring job I've ever seen, Thomas, and I include my own." Everyone laughed, including Thomas, and Priya leaned her head briefly against the seat in front of her, the way tired people do among people they trust.

He counted the hour in his head, because he had never stopped counting. Sixty-three, maybe, or sixty-five if the bus counted. There was no way to be sure, and he found he minded less than he expected to. He took a pretzel, and outside the window the town he was still learning went by, streetlight by streetlight, its names still strange to him. "Next year," Okafor said, "we build the arm twice as strong." "Next year," Thomas said, and ate the pretzel, and waited to find out whether he would still be there when it was true.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: The United Kingdom's standard rate of VAT, a sales tax built into most prices, has been 20 percent since January 4, 2011.
story:
Eva spread the two receipts on the table between the ketchup and the salt, smoothing each one flat with the heel of her hand as though creases were evidence she was destroying. The first was from Ms. Baptiste's diner, where she had worked since March; the second Farah had photographed from her cousin's lunch in Bristol, sent across the ocean at eleven that morning with the message "look at this, it makes no sense."

"Your bill says fourteen pounds even," Eva said. "Mine says fifteen dollars and forty cents, and then GST and PST underneath, so the total is more than the menu price. Yours doesn't show any tax at all."

"Because it's built in," said Aya, wedging herself into the booth with a milkshake she had ordered before sitting down, which was a habit of hers. "It's called VAT." She said it the way one says a word learned abroad, carefully, with the consonants intact.

"Built in where?" Farah leaned over the receipt, close enough that Eva could smell her shampoo. "Like, hiding?"

"Like, in the price. My cousin says it's been twenty percent since the fourth of January, 2011." Aya shrugged. "I looked it up at two in the morning, which is when I do my best arithmetic and my worst everything else."

Eva took out her phone and opened the calculator, because a number like that demanded to be tested. Twenty percent of fourteen pounds was two pounds eighty, so the Bristol lunch had really cost eleven twenty before the tax folded itself invisibly into the menu. Whereas her own grilled cheese had been advertised at fourteen dollars and become fifteen forty at the register, the tax arriving after the fact like an unwelcome guest. She said this out loud, and Farah laughed, and Aya said "the British way is politer but the dishonesty is identical," which nobody could argue with.

Then Eva pulled the other document from her jacket, the one that had actually been keeping her up: her pay stub from the diner, which she had opened three days earlier and stared at for a full minute before going reticent about it, stuffing it in a drawer, and deciding not to think. She had been hired at nineteen dollars an hour. The stub said she had worked sixty-two hours in two weeks and been paid eight hundred and ninety-something, a number that felt like theft until she did the division and found the real culprit listed in small rows beneath: income tax withheld, CPP, EI. Her nineteen dollars had never been nineteen dollars. It had been a gross fiction, the price before the VAT of being an adult.

"So both receipts lie," Farah said slowly, watching Eva's pen move down the stub's columns. "Yours lies downward, hers lies upward."

"I don't think either one lies." Eva was adding the deductions back, checking whether sixty-two times nineteen actually equalled the gross pay printed in the corner. It did, to the cent, which produced in her a small, absurd relief, as if the government might have made an arithmetic error in her favour. "They just show you different parts of the truth. The menu shows what you'd pay in a world with no taxes. The stub shows what you'd keep in a world with no deductions. Neither world exists."

Aya stirred her milkshake with her straw and said that this was the most entropy she had ever heard described over grilled cheese, that the whole system ran on taking tidy numbers and letting them decay into messy ones. Ms. Baptiste came by with the coffee pot, paused at the table covered in paper, and asked whether they were doing homework or an audit. Eva, wanting to propitiate her before she decided it was the latter, turned the stub over and asked the question she had been circling all week: at the end of the year, would she get any of the withheld income tax back?

"That depends on you," Ms. Baptiste said, refilling cups nobody had touched. "File a return and find out. Half the people your age don't bother, and the government keeps it, happily."

Eva looked down at the stub, at the small withheld line, at the Bristol receipt with its tax dissolved invisibly into fourteen pounds. There was a whole machinery under the surface of ordinary numbers, and she had walked over it for years without feeling the gears. She would file the return; she had decided that in the booth, between the ketchup and the salt. What she could not yet say was whether the machinery was fair or merely orderly, and she suspected the answer would take longer than one lunch.

"Send me that receipt," she said to Farah, already photographing her own. "My cousin's, I mean. I'm going to frame them side by side."

Aya raised her milkshake. "To hidden money," she said. "Everywhere."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Under the US Help America Vote Act of 2002, a voter whose eligibility is in question can cast a provisional ballot, which counts only once officials confirm eligibility.
story:
The envelope had been sitting on the kitchen table for three weeks, and Olivia, who was eighteen as of April, had opened it the day it arrived and then left it there like a dare. It was her voter registration confirmation, addressed to her full name, Olivia Reyes-Cardenas, at this address, which was the point, because this address was the thing in question. Her mother said the hyphenated name would cause trouble. Her mother said a lot of things would cause trouble. At sixteen, Olivia had answered by rolling her eyes; at eighteen, she answered by taping the confirmation to the refrigerator, where it hung like a small flag over the leftovers.

That had been September. Now it was the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November, and she was standing in the garage apartment her mother called the in-law suite and her friends called the clubhouse, holding the letter Denzel had slipped under her door two nights ago. Denzel wrote the way he talked, in long tangential spirals that eventually landed somewhere. This one began with a complaint about the school board race, detoured through his uncle's opinions, and arrived at a single underlined sentence near the bottom: "If they give you any grief about the name, don't just walk out, okay? Make them deal with you." She folded the letter along its old creases and put it in her jacket pocket, next to the registration card, and went to find her mother.

The polling place was the community hall two streets over, in the room where Fanny's quinceañero had been held, though today the folding tables held clipboards instead of cake. A poll worker with reading glasses found the letter R in the binder, ran her finger down the column, and ran it down again. "I'm not seeing a Reyes-Cardenas," she said, not unkindly. "I'm seeing a Reyes, Olivia, born in April. Is that you?"

Olivia felt the argument assemble itself in her throat, the whole speech about hyphens and systems and how she was not going to be simplified at a folding table. Then she thought of Denzel's letter, and of her mother, who had once spent an entire afternoon at the DMV refusing to leave until the clerk typed her full name into the computer, and she let the speech collapse into a quieter form. "That's me," she said. "Both of them. The hyphen is the whole point."

The poll worker did not argue, which was its own small surprise. "Okay," she said. "You can vote a provisional ballot." She explained it while filling out the form: under the Help America Vote Act of 2002, a voter whose eligibility was in question could cast one, and it would count only once officials confirmed that the voter was eligible. "So it's a maybe," the poll worker said, and Olivia liked her for saying maybe instead of pretending otherwise.

She filled in the ovals at one of the low tables, in the booth-less openness of the hall, aware of Fanny's mother two rows over and of the man beside her exhaling like the whole country was on his ballot. When she sealed the envelope, she thought of the_dmach arguments from twelfth grade, the ones she used to litigate at lunch with Fanny, who maintained that voting was a ritual and rituals mattered, while Olivia maintained that rituals were what people did instead of fixing things. She had been so certain then. She was less certain now, holding an envelope that might or might not be counted, and she found she didn't mind the uncertainty as much as she'd expected. It felt less like a door closing and more like a diminuendo, an argument softening toward a note she could actually live inside.

Walking home, she texted Denzel a photo of the provisional receipt with no caption, and he replied with a single fire emoji, which she took as sufficient. At the kitchen table, where it had all started, her mother asked how it went, and Olivia said, "I voted a maybe," and watched her mother decide whether to be offended on her behalf.

"They'll check," her mother said finally. "You did everything right." She said it in the voice she used for things she wasn't sure of but wanted to be true, and Olivia, who had spent four years deciding whether to be like her or not like her, sat down across from her and took a piece of the leftover chicken without asking. The confirmation letter still hung on the refrigerator, its corner curling. Her mother reached over and pressed it flat with her palm.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: At a Seder, a piece of the middle matzah called the afikoman is set aside, often hidden for children to find, and eaten as the last food of the meal.
story:
The pavilion smelled of fried plantains and charred brisket, and Katherine had written her grandfather's order of blessings on her palm in ballpoint, which was already smearing. The cultural festival ran until six o'clock, and the organizers had given her family the long table under the east window for the Seder demonstration, one hour, no more, because at six the taiko drummers needed the space. Her grandmother was supposed to have led it, the way she had led it for forty years, but her grandmother was on the fourth floor of St. Anne's with an IV in her arm, and had said, over the phone, her voice thin as onionskin, "You know it, Katherine. You've watched me your whole life."

She had watched, yes, but watching was not the same as standing at the head of a table with thirty strangers and cousins waiting for her voice to tell them what came next. Cristian had come because he came to everything, and he sat at the far end, garrulous as always, narrating the seder plate to the woman beside him, pointing out the shank bone and the bitter herb with genuine delight, which helped somehow, because his enthusiasm made the table feel less like a test. Tyler was there too, sulking a little, having been dragged along and having discovered the dessert table too late to refuse the obligation. Ms. Mendoza, her tenth grade English teacher, stopped by the table on her way to the empanada stand and said, "Katherine, I didn't know this was yours," and stayed, which Katherine both appreciated and resented, because Ms. Mendoza had once eviscerated an essay of hers in red ink, and there was something unbearable about being watched by someone who had seen her fail before.

She began anyway. The blessing over the first cup came out steadier than she expected. The hand-washing, the green vegetable dipped in salt water, the four questions, which her youngest cousin recited in a rush, stumbling on the Hebrew but getting through. Katherine moved down her palm's smeared list, and when she looked up between steps, her mother's face was doing something complicated, half pride and half grief, and Katherine understood that every correct word she said was also a measurement of what was missing.

Then she reached for the three matzot, and her stomach dropped.

She broke the middle matzah, because that was right, that she remembered. She held the larger piece and said, to the table, to herself, "This is the afikoman." The word came out before the plan did. She knew it had to be set aside, that it was hidden for the children to find, and that it had to be eaten as the very last food of the meal, but she had been so careful with the blessings that she had never actually hidden it. The smaller piece sat between the other two matzot where it belonged, and the larger piece sat in her hand like evidence.

Her youngest cousin was already leaning forward, scanning the table legs, the windowsill, the underside of the chafing dish, executing the search with the silent machination of a child who knew there was treasure somewhere and would not be cheated of it. Katherine's mother glanced at the clock. Twenty minutes to six, and the meal could not end without the afikoman, though Katherine could not have said why that rule felt heavier than all the others, only that her grandmother had never once let it slide.

"You forgot to hide it," Tyler said, not cruelly, just factual, from his end of the table.

"I know," Katherine said. Then, to her cousin, "Close your eyes. All the kids, close your eyes, count to thirty in Hebrew or English, dealer's choice." She walked the length of the table while they counted, wondering where in a borrowed pavilion a piece of matzah could possibly belong. On the way she passed Ms. Mendoza, and Katherine, without stopping, tucked it into the folded flap of Ms. Mendoza's canvas tote bag, and Ms. Mendoza looked down at her, and a small understanding passed between them, one conspirator to another, and Ms. Mendoza turned her body slightly so the children could not see.

The search took eleven minutes and involved a false alarm under the tablecloth and a brief diplomatic crisis when two cousins accused each other of peeking. When the youngest finally pulled the afikoman from the tote bag, holding it overhead like a trophy, Ms. Mendoza applauded with the rest, and Katherine paid the ransom she had improvised, chocolate coins from the festival vendor, and the meal finished the way it had to finish, everyone eating a piece of the broken matzah as the last food of the night, the drummers already carrying their instruments toward the pavilion door. Afterward her mother hugged her hard enough to hurt and said, "Call your grandmother. Tell her every detail." Katherine took out her phone outside, in the noise and the frying smell of the emptying festival, and dialed the hospital, holding the last piece of afikoman wrapped in a napkin, still not sure whether she had led the Seder or only performed its outline, and not sure it mattered, because her grandmother's voice, when it came, said, "Did they find it?" and Katherine said, "Every year, Grandma. They always find it."

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: On September 17, 1925, when Kahlo was 18, a streetcar crashed into her bus, leaving injuries that caused her pain for the rest of her life.
story:
Aaron spread the print of The Two Fridas across the picnic table and weighed its corners with kiwis from the bowl, because the wind had opinions about art today. His laptop sat on a stack of old encyclopedias his mother kept for reasons nobody could defend, and beside it, a sheet of Ms. Nielsen's rules: colour, composition, symbolism. Three columns. He was supposed to fill all three by Sunday, and so far column one read "red. also green."

"You're doing it wrong," Alena said, arriving through the gap in the fence the way she always did, without knocking or apology.

"I haven't done anything yet. That's different from wrong."

"You're looking at it like it's a poster. You have to look at it like it's an argument." She dropped onto the bench, took a kiwi, and ate it whole, skin and all, which Martin said was a cry for help and Martin would know, because Martin climbed over the fence two seconds later holding his phone like a torch.

"Okay, history part," Martin announced. "For context. Ready? On September 17, 1925, when Kahlo was eighteen, a streetcar crashed into her bus. The injuries caused her pain for the rest of her life."

"Where'd you get that?" Aaron asked.

"The internet, Aaron. The whole thing is there." Martin set the phone down between the kiwis. "Eighteen. She was our age. Think about that while you two argue about red."

Aaron did think about it, and the thinking had a strange weight. He had been treating the assignment as a puzzle with a right answer, something a grader held in a drawer. But the painting was made by someone who had been sixteen once, standing exactly where he stood, and then a streetcar crossed everything out. The Two Fridas showed a woman doubled, one in European white, one in Tehuana colour, connected by a vein, and one of them was holding scissors. He'd thought the doubling was the point, but now he wasn't sure whether the point was the doubling or the vein.

"She's wearing two costumes," Alena said, tapping the print. "That's a counterpoint, like in music. Two voices, same painting."

"It's more than costumes," Aaron said slowly. "Look at the sky. It's stormy, but she paints it flat, like wallpaper. Almost calm. The outside doesn't match the inside." He wrote flat storm, calm sky in the composition column and felt the small electric pleasure of a sentence that was actually about something.

"You just internalized the lesson," Alena said. "Look at you. Ms. Nielsen would weep."

"I haven't internalized anything. I've written four words." But that evening, after they'd gone, he sat alone in the yard with the solar lights coming on and tried to draft the symbolism column, and the words kept sliding off the page. He understood the vein. He understood the scissors, or thought he did. What he couldn't decide was whether the stormy-flat sky was the world being indifferent, or Frida being indifferent right back.

He texted his aunt, who had actually been to the museum in Mexico City, and she sent him a voice message at eleven that night. He listened to it in the backyard in the dark, holding the phone to one ear, swatting mosquitoes with his free hand. "You're asking the wrong question, cariño," she said. "Stop asking what the sky means. Ask why she made it so quiet when everything else is screaming. Sometimes the flattest thing in a painting is the loudest."

That helped, but it also didn't, because it opened a second question he couldn't close: was he supposed to trust the painting or the painter? The girl in the streetcar, or the woman with the scissors? Sunday morning he typed half a paragraph saying the flat sky represented acceptance, deleted it, typed it again, deleted it again. Finally he kept both sentences, one after the other, and let them sit there contradicting each other on purpose. His aunt's voice and Ms. Nielsen's columns. Martin's fact and Alena's music. He couldn't make them agree, and he was starting to suspect that the disagreement was the assignment.

On Monday he handed it in with the contradiction still in it, plus a final line about the red of the vein and the red of the dress being the same red doing two different jobs, which felt like a discovery even if it might also be obvious. Ms. Nielsen read it at her desk while he pretended to organize his binder.

"You didn't decide," she said.

"No. I mean, I decided not to decide. About that part."

She made a small mark in the margin that he couldn't see, then looked up. "The vein. Tell the class about the vein tomorrow. Five minutes." She slid the paper back across the desk, and there, at the bottom, a single auxiliary comment penciled beside his grade: "Ask better questions in class, please."

"Is that a compliment or an assignment?"

"Yes," she said, and went back to her coffee.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: Particle physicists claim a discovery only at 'five sigma', meaning there is less than a one-in-a-million chance that a random fluctuation alone would produce a signal that strong.
story:
The printer in the corner of the library had been grinding for six minutes, and Elizabeth had counted every page as it slid into the tray, because counting was easier than thinking about what was on them. Ninety-one, ninety-two, ninety-three. Three nights of timing pendulums with a stopwatch app, forty runs per length, and somewhere in the middle of it all a small pattern had appeared: the heavier bob seemed to swing a hair slower than the light one, which every textbook said should not happen. She had checked her arithmetic twice. She had not checked it a third time, because she was afraid the pattern would dissolve the moment she did.

Maxwell dropped into the chair across from her with the specific weight of someone who wanted to be noticed being casual. "Is that your physics thing? Let me see the graph."

She slid one page across, keeping her hand on the corner a second longer than necessary. He leaned in, whistled, and she watched his eyes move from the axis labels to the cluster of points that sat, stubbornly, just below where they belonged.

"That's a real slope," he said.

"It's a small slope."

"Small slopes win science fairs."

Down the table, Dylan looked up from a laptop showing a college financial aid page. "Small slopes also lose science fairs," he said. "Last year a guy claimed plants grew faster if you talked to them. He had a slope. Ms. Delgado took him apart in the Q and A. I've never enjoyed anything more."

"You're a terrible person," Maxwell said, but Dylan wasn't wrong, and Elizabeth knew it. The regional judge two years running had been a retired engineer who asked every finalist the same question: how do you know? She had watched a girl with a beautiful poster about magnets go silent under it, and the silence had been worse than a wrong answer. Ms. Delgado had said something afterward in the hallway, something Elizabeth only half remembered, about a million studies or a million chances, some number so large it had felt abstract, decorative, not germane to anything a seventeen-year-old with a stopwatch could produce.

She found Ms. Delgado at the reference desk an hour later, shelving returns with the resigned efficiency of someone whose student helpers had all abandoned her. Elizabeth put the graph on the desk between a biography of Curie and somebody's interlibrary loan.

"Tell me if this is nothing," she said.

Ms. Delgado looked at it for a long moment. "Tell me what you want it to be."

"That's not fair."

"It's the only fair question. Here's mine. If you ran it again, from scratch, new string, new everything, would those points fall the same way?"

"I don't know. That's the whole problem. I have a slope. I don't know if it means anything."

Ms. Delgado tapped the graph once, not answering, which Elizabeth understood was itself an answer of a kind. The librarian went back to shelving. Elizabeth carried the pages back to the table, where Maxwell was now arguing with Dylan about whether the pendulum result, if real, would be worth a scholarship, and Dylan was saying the word "replication" in the tone of someone who had just learned it and enjoyed saying it.

"I read something last night," Dylan said, turning the laptop around. "Particle physicists won't even say they've found something unless it hits five sigma. Meaning there's less than a one-in-a-million chance a random fluctuation alone could produce a signal that strong. That's their bar. One in a million."

"That's insane," Maxwell said. "Nothing in high school is one in a million."

"That's the point," Dylan said. "That's why nobody announces a particle on a Tuesday afternoon."

Elizabeth sat down slowly. Three nights, forty runs, and a slope that might be anything at all. She thought about the magnet girl's silence, and about Maxwell wanting it to be real, and about how much she wanted it to be real too, and how wanting was exactly the thing you had to interpose something between, some procedure, some distance, or it would eat the data alive. "Then I need to run it again," she said. "Tonight. And then twice more after that."

"You have four days," Maxwell said.

"Then I'll run it four times."

She was gathering the pages when a folded sheet slipped loose from between two of them, a printout she had forgotten she'd made. It was the raw timing log from the second night, and as it drifted to the table she saw, in her own handwriting, that runs eighteen through twenty-three had been recorded in a different pen. She had switched pens at run nineteen, right in the middle of the heavy-bob trials, because the first one had died. She stared at the faint blue of the new ink and felt the slope shift under her, not measurably, not yet, but the way a floor shifts when a house decides to settle.

"Dylan," she said, holding up the sheet. "How much do you like pendulums?"

"Why."

"Because I need a stopwatch, a fresh notebook, and a witness with no stake in the outcome. Same pen all night."

Maxwell groaned. Dylan closed the financial aid page, which for Dylan was practically a standing ovation. "I'll bring the pen," he said. "You bring the string. And if the slope vanishes, I get to tell the engineer judge I helped kill it."

The library lights dimmed for closing as they were still arguing about the bob, and Elizabeth folded the log into her pocket, ink side in, where she could feel it through the fabric all the way home.
